title: One of the best Star Wars films
review:
Haters gonna hate, I guess, but in this case I don't get it. I went into the film with critical eyes, waiting for the cringe to set in. Didn't happen. Went home, read the criticisms and negative reviews. Went to see it again, looking for flaws. Okay, yeah, some of the lines were cheesy. Some of the plot elements were a little far fetched. I wish they'd done more to explain Snoke. But really, none of that made it a bad movie. Maybe nudged it down a star or two, but in the Star Wars franchise, this is a great movie!

Now, I've loved Star Wars since I was a kid. It's basically my religion. However, aside from all the starry-eyed nostalgia, the first few Star Wars films weren't Best Picture material either. Their value was in their mythology and metaphor. So I was happy to see that TLJ stayed true to that vision.

Beyond that, film-wise, this was one of the best Star Wars films ever made. The acting was top notch--equaled only by the performances in Empire. The use of myth and metaphor was very clever, relevant to modern times, and thought-provoking. The character interplay was powerful--especially from my point of view as a woman. The music and cinematography were amazing, and worth seeing in IMAX 3D (which I got the opportunity to do for my second viewing). I am recommending this movie to everyone I know--Star Wars fans or not. It left me with thrills and chills and bouncing out of the theater with a huge smile on my face both times. The whining haters can go to hell, (or re-watch Rogue One, which is kind of the same thing).

title: My family and I loved this movie, and couldn't understand the hate
review: I went to see this with my parents, my older bothers, my sister-in-law and my niece. I am a 37 year-old lifelong Star Wars fan. We have all watched all the films and discussed them all. I kept waiting for this film to disappoint us, and to go home dispirited seeing the franchise ruined. I wanted my family to be with me if that happened. Instead, I found tears of joy in my eyes, and looking over at my father to see him also choking up, because of how beautiful it was. Even my mother and niece, who have been somewhat lukewarm about previous Star Wars films, loved this one, and are looking forward to seeing it again. We honestly went home scratching our heads at why anyone would dislike it. I recently went to see it again in IMAX 3D, and loved it all over again. This is the best Star Wars film I've seen in a long time. FYI, I found Rogue One to be the worse "Star Wars" film and gave that a scathing review. That left a bad taste in my mouth about the direction the franchise might be headed. My faith in Disney was restored with TLJ, and I trust that at least Rian Johnson has kept the vision alive of what makes Star Wars great. Was only saddened and perplexed to see so many people hate on this film.

review:

I could not care less for the casino planet or any of the new characters introduced like Holdo, DJ and Rose. Nor do I care about the struggle of the resistance or the power of the first order since their conflic is just the same as it was in the original trilogy. There is nothing interesting in this movie. They hint at there don't need to be a dark or lightside but in the end there is just that, nothing changes!

Luke ends up being a miserable man whos just waiting to die. Its depressing to watch. Rey is still pretty cool but it never feels like she earns all that powers she has. I dont cared much for Poe in TFA nor did I care much for him in this one. Finns story arc was really good in the last movie but now the story has a hard time finding out what to do with him. I was thinking to myself, is this the dissapointment people felt when they saw Phantom menace?In the end I can't think of any reason to be excited for the next one.

title: Disapointed
review:
This film to me was a huge appointment. After the Mega Successful "The Force Awakens" by JJ ABRAMS was not only a hit with the old fans it also brought in new fans. This film "The Last Jedi" was written and directed by Rian Johnson and he delivered such a boring film that I am in no hurry to see another "Star Wars" movie anytime soon.

This film is sad because it is "Carrie Fisher" last performance. Her daughter (Billie Catherine Lourd) has a part in this but it more or less a glorified "Extra"

In this film the Rebels are at it once again. This time this film ADDS NOTHING NEW OR EXCITING to the franchise. What we get is watered down versions of the newer characters that were introduced in "Force Awakens".

I was hoping for a romance to blossom between "Rey" and "Finn". However that did not happen. I was hoping to find out who the parents of "Rey" were. I was hoping for more "Luke Skywalker". I was hoping to see Lando (Billy Dee Williams). Most of all I missed Harrison Ford.

Luke Skywalker's peaceful and solitary existence gets upended when he Rey, shows up wanting to be trained by a Jedi Master! Luke however no longer believes in the Jedi's.

Meanwhile, Kylo Ren leads the First Order in an all-out assault against Leia and the Resistance.

This story is however part "Empire" and part "Jedi" however it is not very entertaining.

Even though I am in no hurry to see another "Star Wars" film I am happy to hear that JJ ABRAMS is returning for Episode IX. I know the Nerds will thumbs down this review oh well!

I am sure in the years to come this films will be as loved as "Jar Jar Binks"

title: Not the best Star Wars movie ever made, but better than Rogue One and TFA
review:
There are a lot of negative reviews on this movie. And honestly I do not feel it's deserved. While yes, the movie is flawed, it's nowhere near as bad as people make it out to be. The acting is great, the effects are great and when this movie is at it's best it's really up there with A New Hope and Empire Strikes Back. However when it's bad it's as bad as the prequels.

The main plot is also really great. The best thing about it is that you don't know what is going to happen next. When it comes to the subplot, that is proably the weakest part of this movie. I love what the message they are trying to say, but it falls pretty flat.

A lot of people also don't like how Luke Skywalker is in this movie, but I quite liked that they took him in a different direction. The things we learn about him gives him so much more humanity.

All in all, Rian Johnson has created an entertaining Star Wars movie with twists and turns that always have you guessing where the movie is going to go next. ar. I really recommend this one!

title: mini review of Star Wars The Last Jedi
review:
Went to see Star Wars The Last Jedi, I always get sucked in and end up regretting. This one is no exception to that rule. In the words of the immortal Princess Leia, the spark is gone although the budget is still more than handsome and the cash registers are singing happy returns. We know what that means, another sequel to the sequel or to the revamped series after the original and the prequel. It's a sure fire money maker so why bite the hands that feeds you, certainly not George Lucas.
There is one word which kind of sums it all up for me: debris. Lots and lots of debris, especially in 3D it's coming right at you that plus three strands of a story which do not coalesce into a satisfying whole.
One theme endlessly repeated: the light and the dark and who will conquer but meanwhile let's all enjoy the neverending war. Apparently there were cameos of people I missed Lupita N'yongo, Gwendoline Christie plus a wasted Benicio del Toro, an OK. Laura Dern looking suitably gungho and severe in an appropriate outfit.
Still there was something bittersweet knowing that Carrie Fisher's bright light had dimmed but she will be remembered forever here even if the movie itself was a thorough disappointment. Maybe I'm just not a Star Wars fan or I've simply outgrown it. In the end I found it overly long and boring. Once they start shooting each other out of the sky it's hard to tell who the friends and foes are and frankly my dear I don't really give a damn. Reviews have been mostly positive but with all the hype surrounding the release and the hush hush scenario it's not all that surprising. I did enjoy Adam Driver's performance, definitely can hold the screen and one's gaze. His Modigliani face is hard to look away from. My grade: C+

title: A disappointing, but still acceptable sequel in a series trying to find its roots
review:
Director Rian Johnson's Star Wars: Episode VIII - The Last Jedi is easily the grandest and epic film to have come out in 2017. It boasts a balanced cast of series veterans and newcomers along with outstanding production quality. However, what was supposed to be the Empire Strikes Back for the new trilogy has come up short in key areas such as an exciting plot and engaging characters that limit the film from being anything above average.

The Last Jedi picks up immediately after the closing events of Star Wars: Episode VII - The Force Awakens. We cross-cut between Princess Leia leading the Resistance in a desperate escape mission from the pursuing First Order; and Rey trying to recruit a weary Luke Skywalker on his secluded island. On the dark side of the force, Supreme Leader Snoke and Kylo Ren act out plans to try and bring Rey to the dark side.

While the summary I gave makes the film sound simple, it really isn't. There are many side plots and characters that muddy the water and make the overall story meander aimlessly until the final act. Each of the plots feels underdeveloped because of all the juggling and some of them clearly should have been cut or greatly reduced, which would have helped resolve the overlong 150-minute runtime.

The film is also unoriginal and doesn't add anything new or meaningful to the saga. Most everything goes exactly as you would expect, and the things that are different aren't done well. The characters endure many problems within the film mostly because of their own incompetence to do things right. In the end, everything that happened was expected and everything that was new wasn't good.

The biggest problem with the film is how it treats its characters. Rey is still a standout from the previous film and has grown even more since then. She is still trying to make sense of becoming a Jedi but exhibits great bravery and a strong will to help her friends. Luke is hit or miss depending on the scene as he tries to deal with his failures as a Jedi master and Rey's plea for his help in training her. Finn's role is greatly reduced as he becomes part of the supporting cast as he and Rose (a Resistance engineer) embark on a side quest to secure a safecracker. Their plot is totally pointless and neither of them ends up as likable characters by the end of the film as all they do is critique the bad guys and say how things are bad. Kylo Ren and Po are adequate most of the time, but never good enough in their expanded roles. Characters such as Leia, Snoke, and Captain Phasma are either completely disrespected or wasted as Johnson can never seem to figure out what their role should be in the overarching story.

The one thing you can always expect from a Star Wars film is great visuals and an epic lightsaber fight, and The Last Jedi is no exception to that rule. The main lightsaber battle is one of the best in the series and is expertly shot and choreographed for maximum intensity and realism. You can feel the danger and raw power within the characters as they fight for their lives against an unforgiving enemy. The space battle is really well done as well as it blends great visuals and sounds. There is one specific sequence in the latter part of the film that is one of the best looking moments of the year.

While their characters are overall pretty poor, most of the actors do a fine job when it comes to breathing life into the film. Highlights include Daisy Ridley as Rey and Carrie Fisher as Leia. Each of them balances their emotions really well and deliver their lines perfectly in the situation they are thrust in. Mark Hamill does a good job as well at bringing Luke Skywalker back to life after a thirty-year screen absence. He gives Luke the old man treatment but also still reminds us of the headstrong kid we all fell in love with in the original trilogy. Adam Driver is pretty good as Kylo Ren, but he struggles to make his character anything different than what we have already seen.

Some actors, however, don't deserve praise for their work. Both John Boyega and Kelly Marie Tran as Finn and Rose, respectively, make for some pretty forgettable moments in the film that could have been a lot better. They also don't share any chemistry together which makes it hard to care about them the whole time.

Overall, The Last Jedi is a disappointing, but is still an acceptable film in the ever-expanding Star Wars saga. While it isn't the sequel fans were hoping for, it still delivers in getting the look and feel of what a Star Wars film should be.

title: The part that hurts the most...
review:
...is the fact that there were signs of an incredible Star Wars movie buried in this film. It's just completely lost in stupid decisions, dumb character portrayals, and ridiculous plot points. The only time I've ever been this disappointed by a Star Wars movie was after seeing Episode 1 in theaters, but while in my view that movie was just bad through and through, this one could have shined.
First of all, the humor. Humor is not a bad thing in a movie and, in fact, Star Wars generally has good flowing humor between the characters. The problem with the humor in this one is it's not character interaction so much as it is just cheap jokes. There's one at the beginning of the movie in which Poe is acting like there's a communication problem between him and General Hux which makes no sense whatsoever in this universe. In order for that joke to work you have to accept that their technology is no always reliable, but in Rogue One we saw that ships could communicate while in hyperspace, you mean to tell me that their technology may not work ship to ship while next to each other?
Second: Canto Bite. This sequence was so out of place, and it actually showed to be pointless to the story. I think my biggest problem is Canto Bite feels too much like Las Vegas but with people masquerading as aliens. Slot machines and I'm pretty sure they were playing craps. Come on. Where is the imagination here? It's not like you have to go very far, there are tons of references of gambling games in books and other media, but instead it's basically a standard casino from earth. Lame. Did I mention that this whole subplot had no purpose? Yeah, because it didn't.
I honestly could ramble on about this, but I'm just going to stop. This COULD have been an awesome Star Wars movie, but it was lost in some of the dumbest decisions ever made. I'm not even sure if I care about seeing the next Star Wars movies which makes me incredibly sad.

title: Not as bad as the prequels, not as good as the original trilogy, somewhere in between...
review: "Star Wars Episode VIII: The Last Jedi", from "Looper" director Rian Johnson, is the latest entry in the "Star Wars" franchise and does it live up to the hype? For me, sadly, this 8th episode was a bit of a disappointment. Sure, it offers some good performances from Daisy Ridley, Mark Hamill and Adam Driver, it has some pretty cool action scenes,the score from John Williams is expectedly good and in my opinion slightly better than the score for "The Force Awakens", the CGI is decent, there's some good camera work and for the 2 hour and 32 minute run time the pacing is not terrible. For me what made "The Last Jedi" a bit of a disappointment was for one thing that it felt all too safe and family friendly. There were moments throughout the film where I thought the filmmakers would take some risks, but just ended up going the predictable and at times cheesy route. There were even a few times where I remember thinking to mysely "Wow, is that actually going to happen?", but then it didn't or something else happened and possible major events were avoided. There wasn't all that much tension throughout the run time either and I left the cinema rather underwhelmed and the film failed to leave an impact. Despite really wanting to love the film considering I'm a "Star Wars" fan myself, I just couldn't really wrap my head around the overly long 152 minute run time and the needless sub-plots, especially the side quest with Finn that constantly slowed down the pace, took up way too much time and overall just didn't need to be there. The comedy doesn't always work and is mostly child-oriented, especially the introduction to the creatures found on the Ahch-To island known as "Porgs" that are basically there to boost merchandise sales and don't really play into the story much at any point. Another thing that surprised me was how much Princess Leia Organa, played by Carrie Fisher (Rest In Peace) in her last portrayal of the character, didn't have to do with the story. Aside from 1-2 short scenes, Leia was, in my opinion, kind of wasted and could've been utilized a lot more. Talking about the supporting cast, there aren't any standouts, the best performances are definitely those from Ridley, Hamill and Driver, the rest just aren't as strong, new characters don't leave an impact and returning characters were more enjoyable to watch in "The Force Awakens". Negatives aside, I still think you can watch "The Last Jedi", it isn't a complete failure, it has its entertaining moments and is enjoyable to watch (especially with friends and/or the family) if you're not expecting too much and there are definitely some funny moments and homages to the older films that will probably make fans crack a smile. It's clear that Rian Johnson is a big fan of the franchise and wants to make the best kind of "Star Wars" film that he can, but in comparison to J.J. Abrams's previous effort, I think "The Last Jedi" just doesn't hold up. All in all, I'm kind of disappointed with "Star Wars: The Last Jedi", maybe it was due to the high expectations I had for the film, but it just didn't do it for me. It felt way too family friendly, the subplots are mostly unnecessary and could have been easily cut out, the film isn't that rewatchable and it just seemed a bit rushed to name a few things. The scenes between Rey, Luke Skywalker and Kylo Ren were definitely the most interesting to watch in the entire film and those actors definitely gave the best performances. The action scenes were also entertaining with the decent camera work and CGI, but I feel the majority of the film was overall still just rather lackluster and played it too safe. The supporting cast isn't as strong as the main cast and some of the interesting plot points established in the previous film, for example where and who Rey's parents are, feel like they are just thrown away in this sequel. Although not quite as terrible as the prequels, this is definitely not one of the best "Star Wars" films to ever come out and I would say it's pretty much as good as "Rogue One", if not, a little better.

title: Pretty much what I expected, and that's fine.
review:
So this one was dumb, silly, goofy, contrived and in some cases pretty flawed... and yet that's what a Star Wars movie is.

Star Wars is not a perfect franchise by any means at all; I haven' given any of the movies above a 7 so far. They're dumb, silly fun in space. This one's better than the last two (Rogue One and The Force Awakens), but it's not quite as good as Empire Strikes Back. So what?

It was fun, shot very well, had tonnes of character, lovely callbacks and memorable moments. That's all I want from a Star Wars movie, and also what I was expecting.

Pretty much all of the backlash is made up of nostalgia- blinded 20 year old fans who hold the original trilogy up on the highest pedestal they can erect. Sure, the original three were groundbreaking at the time and shaped Hollywood for the better and worst, but none of them are masterpieces, or even come close; they're just dumb fun with an added dash or mysticism and classic Hollywood romanticism. Nothing more, nothing less.

TLJ was just as fun, but also as dumb, AND THATS OK. 7/10

title: This movie is about failure. That's not ironic.
review:
This movie really struggles to get across its themes. It has commendably bold themes, but it juggles plot threads like Jar Jar Binks in its painful-to-watch attempts to portray them. Subtlety is a foreign concept here. In the end the narrative settles for throwing everything on the floor and telling you what it was trying to do via characters spelling it out for you when in actuality very little holds up to such estimations.

Tone, pacing, structure, you name it, this movie screwed it up. Any scene you're prepared to take seriously is probably going to slap you in the face with a poorly placed joke for having such rational expectations; many of which will long outstay their welcome after nailing the comedic timing with the accuracy of a storm trooper. Important scenes come and go with little time to really sink in, especially on the first viewing, and most of the run time is delegated to long, drawn out subplots; which tie into the third act through such baffling contrivances it feels like a bad dream. The only thing that really matters in the third act is a spontaneous conversation between two characters who had little to do with anything throughout the rest of the story. Everything else leads to a dead end or worse.

Don't get me wrong; the structure is a hefty rock balanced on a stick and called a hammer, but a lot happens in this movie. There is certainly a lot of change by the time the credits roll. Episode IX could be anything... anything but a rehash of Episode VI. The Last Jedi beats it to the punch: a few key scenes are ripped directly from Return of the Jedi, one of which is almost literally fast-forwarded in comical fashion. At least the efforts to subvert these scenes will leave you dumbfounded, one way or another.

The acting is top notch, but it's kind of hard to tell when many characters are too stubborn, stupid, and illogical to relate to. Dialogue is without a doubt one of the few joys in this film; if the characters aren't cracking cringe inducing jokes with the misdirection of a 5 year old trying to hide the bubblegum they stole from the checkout shelf at the store, they're eloquently debating different points of view. And there are a few witty lines here and there that made me laugh without hating myself, so the humor isn't all bad. If most of the humor works for you, you'll likely feel more forgiving for the rest of the film's underwhelming elements.

But for dedicated long-term fans, there are very few of the down to earth human moments the franchise is known for to keep you grounded during this flight through abstract human allegory and externalization. There are some emotionally potent beats that will undoubtedly do the trick for some viewers, but for those of us who need something substantial supporting those beats to stay invested in them, we're left empty-handed.

Special effects are absolutely stunning, as always. However, most of the set designs are oddly generic and uninspired - which has never been a problem before in this franchise. There's a moment where Finn expresses awe at a certain setting and I can't help but recoil in embarrassment at how unsuited a reaction it is.

There's some really cool, innovative, and visually impressive action sequences, but the standard action scenes you might traditionally expect are either lackluster or missing altogether.

There are some plot twists that are pretty sure they're smarter than you are, and are almost by nature rubbing your face in how smart it is. The cinematography takes your nose to some dark places to make sure you know, this movie is smarter than your dumb fan theories, and it relishes every second it has your face lodged in its nether regions. Personally, my big take away from all this is insulted intelligence... not that I think I'm particularly smart, but I don't feel these subversions are as clever as they fancy themselves. Some might find these exciting, others will not be impressed.

The biggest thing this movie attempts to do is expand the Force. It simultaneously passes with flying colors and fails in a spectacular dumpster fire of a mess. It's three most prominent instances of Force abuse are haphazard, cheap, and tasteless, almost certain to paste the toes of fans who hold any reverence for the fictional entity that makes this galaxy far, far away so unique. In other instances, more integral to the plot, the expansions build on preexisting established lore in a logical and satisfying manner, ripe with mystery and intimacy between you and the characters exploring these new facets - marking the most investment I had watching this film.

Overall, this movie is a pretentious attempt at subverting the Star Wars saga as a whole, and only really succeeds at showing us why Star Wars is great through an example of what-not-to-do. It's sloppy, like a kid playing with his toys. Before long he is taken by passion and whim, abandoning any sense of logic or introspective to have fun pretending he's crafting a compelling story, only to let the passion die out of eventual boredom, and forget every ridiculous thing that just transpired in his hands to go back to the well of deep and inspired stories that inspired such passion in him in the first place.

This is a depressing example of why Star Wars fans don't make Star Wars movies. Or rather now why they shouldn't be allowed to. Rian Johnson has an interesting imagination, but it got the better of his cognition in this particular film-making effort... and I can't blame him. This is fan-fiction, quickly and excitedly sprawled out on a canvas, unchecked and unhinged. Had it been thought through more rationally in the writing phase, maybe these ideas could have yielded an amazing and fresh Star Wars film, but this is sadly just not the case here.

title: An overall lame plot packed with incompetent heroes and villains.
review:
I'll keep this short because I want this review to be spoiler free.

title: Extraneous plots and Characters turn this into a mess.
review:
I signed up to IMBD just to rate this film 2* and help bring its overall rating down. I just don't see what critics saw in this film to give it such rave reviews other than fear of not getting exclusives on the next Disney franchise. Rogue One is the best action Sci-Fi I've ever seen and love it, Force Awakens has an excellent tone and menacing darkness throughout although it has a few flaws. The Last Jedi... what a complete mess. Adam Drivers Performance is stunning and he alone brings some class to the film. https://tt.amazon.com/0141457590

The list of extraneous characters in this movie is baffling; Fin, LUKE SKYWAKER, Po, BB8, Vice Admiral Holdo, Snoke, Chewbacca, Captain Phasma, Maz, Rose and DJ. There is not one character on this list who's potential isn't completely wasted and their deaths (Holdo maybe an exception though if she had been a spy for the First Order it would have been a million times more interesting) utterly devoid of meaning and relevance both on a personal level with the characters or with regard to the grand narrative.

The James Bond villain Captain Phasma having gotten out of the trash compactor and got off Star Killer base returns to give Fin and Rose every chance to escape rather than just execute them. The evilness of the First Order is never explored and their merciless execution would have been a defining moment in the film possibly giving some meaning to Fin and Rose's (otherwise extraneous) plot.

Vice Admiral Holdo... Should have been a really interesting role and potential new leadership for the rebels but Laura Dern was given a horrible script (Phantom Menace-esk), her actions made literally no sense or she never explained to Po WHY she was withholding information from other than to create something for Po to do as his character is kicking around for something to do. Her ending while brave etc etc had no emotional punch as the audience have no stake in her story, a similar thing happens with Snoke meaning his death is simply a means of getting Kylo Wren on the throne and getting rid of Snoke who's sudden appearance in the last film made things awkward.

Luke... Wow compare Luke's Arc with Rick Deckard's narrative arc in Blade Runner 2049. Deckard's conflicted nature remains enthralling and centrally relevant to plot while clearly moving on and maturing since the original film. Luke Skywalker's cowardice is painful for any Star Wars fan and his death is just meh. How was that ALLOWED to happen?!

DJ had the potential to be a fascinating character showing people who exist within the framework of the whole conflict and who's complicity allows the First Order to thrive. Del Toro did a sterling job making the most of the pitiful amount of screen time he was given. Surely the 'Singapore Donkey Podrace' scene could have been scrapped for more of this characters story and motivations.

I will make a special mention of Adam Driver, his deeply conflicted character literally held the space-time continuum of this film together.

title: Controversial Redemption, and Evolution.
review:
STAR WARS IX TLJ REVIEW: *WITH SPOILERS*

I FELT CONFLICTED COMING OUT OF THE THEATER, LIKE SO MANY AVID STAR WARS FANS DID. I HAVE COMPILED MY THOUGHTS INTO THIS REVIEW AND I HOPE THEY CAN BRING SOME PEACE TO THE MINDS OF MY FELLOW STAR WARS FANATICS.

This film is about Luke's Redemption. I know... sounds crazy but read on. Basically, As those who have seen it know, Luke nearly killed his nephew for fear of him killing younglings (in contrast, earlier in his life he saved his father who was a genocidal murderer).

Question: Is it not possible for him to do both at different times in his life? (Forget the argument of "it's not in his character") He had a thought of fear in which he regretted a moment later. Is it not possible for even the strongest men to have weak points? OF COURSE IT IS. Even the greatest men who have been held on the highest of pedestals have made mistakes, or at least considered them. And oh boy, Luke igniting his signature green lightsaber was one helluva mistake.

It is completely natural for "the Legend", the GOOD man, THE Luke Skywalker to feel like a hypocrite. He felt like he had betrayed his personal beliefs and himself. The one thing he cared for, his family and the growth of "good" in the galaxy, had been uprooted because of his moment of weakness. Therefore He exiled himself. He questioned everything he knew.

The turning point was Rey coming to Ach To and annoying him to the point of training. (Although his only training was a few meager words in an attempt to dissuade Rey from learning about the Jedi ((which he failed)) it inevitably opened him up) The pivotal point in the film is after Rey leaves. Jedi Master Yoda appears and tells Luke the truth about his shortcomings with Ben Solo and his failures. Yoda exlaims: "The greatest teacher, failure is..." This final lesson kicks him hard. He picks himself up and restores his fractured hope. Luke realizes that he made a mistake but he was wrong and he cant give up hope.

He then appears before the First Order in a force-hologram and allows the remaining members of the resistance a chance to escape and fight another day. AND HE DIES... My original thought was this: I wish Luke didn't die, and perhaps that still stands. But if we are talking about his specific moment of death, would he have had enough time to travel to Crait to protect the resistance and efficiently create enough time for their escape? (Also with the AT-AT fire: in person he couldn't have stopped that barrage, lets be real)

Note: Remember how much effort it took Yoda to lift the Fuel canister about to fall on Anakin/ Obi Wan after the Dooku fight in Attack of the Clones or lifting the X-Wing in ESB? If those comparibly small actions tired out the arguably strongest force user of all time, then it makes sense that Luke would die from projecting himself clearly across the galaxy. In the end, He selflessly sacrificed himself to ensure the survival of the resistance, also saving, in his words "the Last Jedi": Rey. If the sacrifice of himself for the continuation of the Jedi and the Resitance isnt Redmeption for Luke, then what is?

SOME CONS: 1. A Star Chase was the best plot to be used? 2. Admiral HOLDO not telling Poe is dumb and creates a useless side-plotline. Only reason I can think of for Poe/ Finn/ Roses plot is to introduce the planet with the force sensitive children and to involve the three in the film. Otherwise the scenes are pointless. Take out those scenes and the film is shorter, more intense, and significantly improved. 3. No Snoke backstory

  • IN CONCLUSION -


Luke/ Rey/ Ben's story along with the force-sensitive children at the end make this movie exciting and bring new elements as well as the "all-bets-are-off" mindset for Episode IX. Ben Solo managed to do something even Vader couldn't (control the galxy, nearly). The possibility of Rey leading a new Jedi Temple is intriguing. (I DO HOPE LUKE RETURNS AS A FORCE-GHOST to guide Rey. Although, YODA did say she had all she needed to become a Jedi, so this may not happen.)

Maybe I'm a hopeless Star Wars fanatic trying desperately to cling onto the franchise. Maybe I'm trying to see the best out of Rian Johnson's film. It's clear what plenty of fans and critics think. This is my opinion, take it for what it is.

This is one fact about my opinion: I am trying to open my mind to the outcomes and possibilities of this storyline. That in itself is much more than most of the fans of this sci-fi franchise are ironically uncapable of doing. At first I was dissapointed with most of the film, but now I am looking at it without the opinions of others affecting me. I remember feeing confused after seeing it, wondering if i should hate it or like it or love it. I have compiled my thoughts into this review. I dont hate it, I dont love it. But I like it and I respect it. I am looking forward to episode 9, in two long years from now, so far far away.

title: Illusion about Trilogy
review:
I gave it only 3 stars and that was more then generous. People used to argue about prequels, but comparing to them, this "trilogy" is utter pile of attempts how to destroy one of the most successful movie franchise ever.

I am using quotation marks, since there is no trilogy here. There is no 6-8 hours story smartly divided on 3 movies like it was done in both previous trilogies so far. I am wondering did Mr. Rian Johnson even watched the Force Awakens movie before making this one.

title: I felt a great disturbance in the force. As if millions of voices suddenly cried out in terror
review: Where does one begin to describe all this is wrong with this chapter of the story. And let me remind everyone that from the very start, way back in 1977, this has always been a Skywalker story. Episodes 4-6 of the original trilogy were about Luke Skywalker. Or worse, we've been kicked into the sarlacc pit to die a long miserable death reliving every awful moment of this movie.

title: The Last Jedi or.....Harry Potter In Outer Space
review:
STAR WARS: THE LAST JEDI. Middle films in trilogies can bring some wonderful movies - GODFATHER II and EMPIRE STRIKES BACK are key examples. But, they can also be problematic - see IRON MAN II and ATTACK OF THE CLONES. Unfortunately, THE LAST JEDI falls closer to the latter than the former. Since everyone reading this has likely seen JEDI, no need for a summary. Suffice it to say that it picks up right after THE FORCE AWAKENS and ends up with a lot of open strands and questions.

What JEDI does right is the production design, tech elements and the photography (mainly on 35mm film). John Williams' music is decent, if uninspiring. Daisy Ridley is a rising young actress, even if she is given precious little to do here (much the same can be said about John Boyega and Adam Driver). Kelly Marie Tran's Rose is a refreshing new character. Unfortunately, the same can't be said for Vice Admiral Holdo. Laura Dern is a fine actress but she simply doesn't command here. She essentially gets rolled by Poe (Oscar Isaac) and then smiles and says, "I like him" (no wonder the resistance is in such trouble if treason is smiled upon). Unfortunately, Carrie Fisher clearly shows the signs of her failing health, and isn't able to be her usual vigorous presence. Still, the worst newcomer comes in the form of 'Benicio Del Han Solo'. DJ is such an obvious Han Solo/Lando Calrissian copy that even Del Toro seems bemused by the character. I half-expect DJ to be visited by the ghosts of Han and Lando in the next installment.

Most of those deficiencies wouldn't matter as much if the whole were more riveting. Unfortunately, Writer/Director Rian Johnson has so many subplots going on that none of the characters, including the supposed main ones, is ever given the screen time to breathe despite the 152 minute length. The battle scenes are numbingly bland - no more compelling than an average Star Trek TV episode. The Casino sequence is technically well-handled, but the more realistic setting feels out of place in the fantasy universe of Star Wars. It simply doesn't feel like anything else in the previous eight features.

The Force has, obviously, been a part of the series since the beginning. Still, it never felt as much a part of the sorcery and magic world as it does here. The Leia floating through space and the Rey/Snoke/Kylo mind-meld threatened to turn this into Harry Potter In Outer Space at times. Maybe Rey can just dispense with the Light Saber next film and just wield a wand.

I've saved my biggest critique for last: Luke. Unlike those who have ripped JEDI for abandoning the 'canon', I had no problem with the new perspective on the character. I'm not wedded to any particular interpretation of the character or the larger story. Unfortunately, the movie does a mediocre job of elucidating it's take. More directly, the part needed a better performance for this most critical of roles. I have always like Mark Hamill. I've enjoyed the times I have been in his presence at Comic-Con and other Cons. He seems like one of the good guys in the business. But, there is a reason why he never became an A-List star despite once being one of the most famous actors in the world. Hamill isn't bad, but he is underwhelming. With that void at the center, JEDI never can take flight. All of the other issues of convoluted story and pacing are magnified.

JEDI isn't a bad film, simply a disappointing one. With the goodwill from FORCE AWAKENS more was expected. There IS a reason why so many fans have been dispirited by the picture (yes, there were some organized naysayers, but the volume of displeasure is so large that it can't be denied that it is much more than a pinpointed 'conspiracy'). Hopefully, the next entry will have a more cohesive tale to tell.

title: This is not the move you are looking for.(waves hand)
review:
I watched The Last Jedi on the first weekend it came out. I went in fresh not hearing any reviews and having little expectation on what it would be besides some continuation of story and character arcs and from The Force Awakens, which I thought was a decent movie. I loved Rouge One because the of depth of the well written and executed story. I have enjoyed all the Star Wars movies and shows I have watched, even the one other people criticized like the prequels, until now.

When I left the theater I wasn't sure how I felt about the movie. The visuals and sound were stunning. Some of the acting was good, some even great in my opinion. The problems that left me conflicted were the massive and multitude of plot holes, incoherent story, and unnecessary and poorly thought out plot devices. It took some time for me to process the movie and as I did I started to slowly hate what I had saw. It's not that I mind change, gotcha style(of which this had plenty of) movies, or a new direction for the franchise. It is the direction this takes the franchise that is the problem. I now understand why Mark Hamill was some what cryptically critical of this movie in interviews I have watch since.

From the way some characters were killed off to basically breaking established(even accepted by Disney) or taking liberty with cannon, The Last Jedi trashes all the movies that came before and burns them down. Rian Johnson even seems to intentionally destroy story work established by Abrams in the last movie. Open story arcs and character building are smashed and unanswered questions are made irrelevant or treated with contempt.

There are a lot of SJW messages in this movie. I remember hearing years ago that Kathleen Kennedy(Lucas Films president) is a rabid feminists and misandrist which could explain some of the choices made. In general male characters in the movie are painted in a bad light. Women are painted more as heroes, which is fine but not at the expense men which is just sexist. The movie goes out of its way injecting an entirely(and unnecessary) sub plot just to make sociopolitical commentary. Most people enjoy scifi and fantasy as an escape from every day life and be inspired, not to get overt political commentary and sexism.

If you like flashy effects, ok acting, and good sound you may like the movie. If you like good story structure, coherency, and/or congruence my advice is to wait till it's free on TV because in my opinion it's not worth paying to see.

title: Not a bad movie, but not a great one
review:
For all of those who feel betrayed, disappointed, and upset (I can relate) this movie is not a 1, 2, or 3 stars out of 10. No matter how you look at it the movie is not that bad. Please be honest/realistic when you rate instead of lashing out in anger.

Now the movie. Did I enjoy it? Yes. Was it at all what I was expecting? No. However it doesn't have to be nor should it. The special effects, music, costumes, and choreography during the fight scenes were awesome. The set locations were some of the best we've seen in a while. I loved the salt planet even if it did seem a little too Empire Strike Back in its use.

As for the story it starts out great, but for me when we got to the scene where Leia floats through space is when it started to drag, and leave me questioning some of the decisions and direction. Now everything from there isn't bad, it's just hit or miss, or for lack of a better term poorly executed.

For example I don't have an issue with Snoke dying (if in fact he is dead), but for a sith supposedly as powerful as he's presented to be he gets taken out pretty easy. If anything his death is premature. IMO an example of poor execution. If he can do things such as connect Rey, and Kylo across the vastness of space, feel every intention, thought of Kyle through the force then how come he can't feel him using the force right in front of him, or the lightsaber moving.

Another issue for me that ties into this is Kylo use of the force. I was never sold on his abilities, or him being as powerful as Snoke states he is. Is he powerful yes, but it's not how he uses the force, but his attitude/behavior that kills it for me. Plus the fact that he is bested by an untrained scavenger in the TFA that I'm just not sold he can best Snoke.

Speaking of Kylo he seems to have matured since TFA, and for the most part he has. I enjoyed his character throughout the movie. The dialogue between him and Rey especially. It's not until the end before he fights Luke that he regresses back into emo Vader acting like a adolescent teen.

Moving on I was disappointed with the lack of character development for Finn. He was one of my favorite characters in TFA, but in this movie no character development until the end when he tries to sacrifice himself. No additional backstory, and like the first movie he starts out tr to run away.

Rose? Not a bad character. I enjoyed her character introduction , and interaction with Finn in the beginning, but ultimarely her character left me bored.

Talking about these two the Vegas scene didn't bother me with the casino, animals, and little kids. What did bother me was them being thrown in prison with all there clothing, a wrist watch to get the current reading on fuel consumption oh and a coder who still has all his clothing, and hidden tools who decides not to break out until Finn and Rose show up. Huh? Again poor execution.

Now our two other main characters. Rey. My biggest issue with this film is we have built SO much mystery and hype surrounding her parentage. First we have the scene in the dark side cave on the island. Which was pretty cool by the way only to be left disappointed when the reflection is her? Ok fine keep teasing us. Then we finally make it to that moment when Kylo states he knows and prods her to say it that we get our answer...junkers....nobodies. Really!?! That's the best we could do. So anti climatic and very infuriating for everyone who's waited 2 yrs. Sorry but this was the biggest disappointment of the film. I was angry. No I don't expect Rey to be related to some great Jedi, or Sith, but nobodies? IF that is the where were going then there is no way she could have done what she did in TFA without training. No Jedi has ever done it before her.

Finally Luke. My favorite character in this movie besides Rey and Kylo. He did a great job bringing Luke to life. I especially loved the flashbacks of younger Luke during the temple scenes with Kylo. The force projection was especially cool and a unique take on the force. The scene with Yoda was an awesome surprise, and handled well.

With that said this isn't Luke. The handling of his character could/should have been different. Do I have a problem with him dying? Absolutely not. It's necessary in order to usher in a new era and push the story forward. Just like it was necessary for Han to die in order to send Kylo over the edge and fully to the dark side. I just hate the way executed it. Luke instead of owning up to his mistake (was it really his mistake or anything he could do?) is reduced to a miserable nomad who is in hiding and just wants to die.

Again very anti climatic since we built up all this mystery about there being an awakening in TFA (Rey), and R2-D2 coming to life to finish the map with BB8. Like Luke knew it was time in TFA. However any of that story is tossed aside like it never happened. One final question? Why was Luke's lightsaber blue in the final battle? I know it's nitpicking but that baffled me.

I could go on, but this review is already long enough. Ultimately the explanation of Rey's parents, poor treatment of Finn, Luke, and the confusing or should I say glaring plot holes killed it for me. A lot of the groundwork laid out in TFA is just ignored, or never explained. In the end this movie left me amazed, conflicted, nostalgic, but ultimately disappointed. I am really not excited about Episode IX. In fact this is the first time I'm seriously considering not purchasing The Last Jedi when it comes out on Blu-Ray.

title: Missed Opportunities
review:
The movie can most simply described as a series of seemingly unrelated, yet aesthetic, short stories that Disney idea-vomited out without any intention of weaving them into a more meaningful plot. Minus 2 big characters and a TON of resistance ship passengers who hold no emotional attachment from the audience (well except Admiral "Trap God" Ackbar, R.I.P.), the movie leaves off right where it started: a scarce resistance army fleeing the endless first order horde.

A good story must have a seemingly impossible obstacle for the protagonists to overcome so that the audience gets maximum satisfaction out of that moment when that story's Luke finally finds a way to beat that story's unstoppable Vader. There is this universe-wide mutual agreement that the first order is kicking ass, which is confusing because of the consistent on-screen losses the First Order racks up. We don't actually see any of these First Order victories unless you count the blowing up of endless resistance ships mentioned above. The Dark Side has become so feeble that we don't even enjoy when Finn beats Phasma or Kylo and Rey stab Snoke in the back. Snoke is the only formidable villain in the movie and he falls victim to a swoop of the force that Brutus would be proud of. Phasma, who so many fans were excited about, loses again in a familiar confrontation with the defected stormtrooper who previously refused to fire his blaster (at least she didn't give away the codes without hesitation this time). I want to see Kylo use that pubertal anger on something other than a control panel. I want to see him furiously lay into a relevant resistance character. Through two movies, Finn is the only character Kylo has beaten fair and square. Yet, he continues to strike down potent characters when they are not looking. The trailers suggested Rey's flirtation with the dark side and I don't really see what that weird mirror scene had to do with the dark side at all. I was expecting some 'deal with the devil' situation where the dark side offered her the answers she was looking for if she only join them, creating a struggle within Rey. Don't even get me started on First Order General Bill Weasley.

Luke is the face of the Star Wars franchise. Even at the end of The Return of the Jedi, Luke's power is still raw and untamed. The possibilities for seasoned veteran jedi master Luke Skywalker were endless, but Luke's new Disney persona (openly detested my Hamill himself before Disney paid him to take it back) only added another tween EMO personality to a trilogy that already had one too many to start with. The whole island plot disappoints because it failed to convincingly explain the Jedi's hypocrisy- they were self-proclaimed peacemakers, but they conveniently got to choose when and how the republic finally achieved "peace". This was already thoroughly explained in the prequels. Rey's "training" consisted of Luke telling stories of his regrets and creepily gazing at her backside while she swung a lightsaber at a rock. Surely they could've incorporated some feeling of enlightenment in the force or where she fits into the force's plan. Despite my disappointment in Luke, scenes of him with Leia, R2 and Chewie were enjoyable and he looked awesome!

I wasn't sold on Finn originally but I convinced myself to give him a chance past TFA. He proved himself to be increasingly detrimental to the new trilogy. He is the main source of this frequent forced humor that TLJ has gotten a lot of heat for. Limit the humor to Chewie, the droids and the little puffin-hamsters. Letting Finn sacrifice himself right when he finally was close to seeing Rey would have been perfect dramatic irony. He is also part of the most inconsequential, politically motivated subplot Star Wars has ever seen. The whole Canto Bight casino subplot achieved absolutely nothing except for the development of this awkward love triangle with Rose (who no one gives a damn about) and Rey. Apparently having an overkill of racial and gender diversity among the protagonists and almost entirely white men opposing them wasn't enough so they threw in some attacks on the upper class and a dash of animal cruelty as well..? Extremist views are even glorified when Finn says, "It was worth it though, to tear up that town, make 'em hurt." This same town he was in awe of until Rose told some sob story about a group of people (not even the exact same people!) that she assumed were just like the guests at the casino. They just stole Benicio del Toro's 'collector' character from Guardians of the Galaxy and slapped a lisp on him. Absolutely nothing was added to the big picture from these story arcs.

This leads me to the main problem of this movie: they were afraid to take risks! It was almost like they wanted to, but took the easy way out at the last second. They tease a battle between Luke and Kylo that quickly turns into a force projection cop out. If Luke is going to die anyway, why not have him be present for it? Take a risk! The battle in the throne room was awesome and set the stage for limitless opportunities for twists and turns, but instead, Kylo and Rey band together against the praetorian guard just to... go right back to the same side that they started. Take a risk! The praetorian guard were impressive additions and put up a sufficient fight, but their leader is already dead so I'm confused on why they're fighting at all. The flashbacks to Kylo's turn at Luke's jedi school entailed no events that we couldn't have predicted after TFA. Take a risk! Snoke was pure evil, had the potential to be the first strong dark side character, and instilled curiosity about his identity, his motivations, and his role in Kylo's turn. They decide to answer none of these questions and give him a pathetic death. Take a risk! O I forgot they did take a big risk, by having Leia survive in space and perform a 1970's style Superman float back to the cockpit, securing the dumbest scene in Star Wars history. I'm convinced the Leia space scene and the whole casino situation were meant for deleted scenes in the DVD release that they just forgot to take out.

I had a lot of problems but there was no doubt the movie had its moments. Poe (Oscar Isaac) was awesome even if his first scene surviving taking out all of the turrets on a star destroyer was a little absurd. Isaac and Carrie Fisher really built in each other in the scenes that they shared. I loved the Yoda scene. Rey and Kylo's scenes together were gripping. BB8 never disappoints. Admiral Holdo, The successor to Leia, had a strong character progression that had you rooting against her to start only to show herself more and more likeable throughout the movie.

title: Fairly Schmeh
review:
I wanted to give myself time to sort out my thoughts on this film, and see what others had to say, which seem to be on-par with my feelings, which aren't good. If I were to use two words to describe this film it would be disappointing and boring. I had high hopes for this film since The Force Awakens was good and I loved Rogue One. This, while not a total train wreck just did not have much going for it in way of story, plot, excitement, fun. The script was just terrible. Full of holes, all over the place, meandering and lifeless. This SW edition definitely ranks around the bottom for me with Phantom Menace and Attack of the Clones, which were nothing more than long toy commercials. If anyone were to ask me if they should see it I would suggest they see Jumanji instead, which was entertaining, funny, and a lot more fun.

The only two characters in this film I was remotely interested in were Rey and Kilo Ren. And given the large number of characters in this film, that is not a good thing. Rey and Kilo had the only interesting storyline that had any tension whatsoever. And their fight scene with the guards was probably the only bright spot. The Poe storyline was reckless and did nothing to convey him as a competent character. Why wasn't he thrown in the brig or shot out of the airlock like they do to traitors on Battlestar Galactica? The story presented these strong female leaders then reduced Leia and Holdo to these motherly types who think an adult tantruming and acting like an idiot is likable? Poe acting out of impulse instead of thinking got most of their remaining fleet killed all to destroy one measly ship, then after that he continued to disobey orders and tried to do a coup and take over the ship. What leader would think that's adorable??? I was happy to see Laura Dern but then they just reduced her to the typical roll women usually play in films as either sex objects to bolster the men or their mothers.

I did not understand the point of the Rose character. Her sister who died would have made a lot more sense and I was actually disappointed when she was killed. She would have complimented Rey's character and made a much better love interest for Finn, and maybe created some kind of love triangle tension with Rey, who did not seem to care one bit by Finn's affection for Rose. Which, understandable that Rey, the uber Jedi is not going to be threatened by a rando fleet grunt. The only thing I could figure was this was some Disney notes where they wanted Rose and Finn to play the Timon and Pumba of the film, the two bumbling comedic relief to compliment the hero, which is fine for Disney but not appropriate for SW.

I liked Finn in first film and thought he had an interesting backstory, but he just seems to be going nowhere other than aimless adventures, and following Rey around like a pathetic puppy. Basically, there's no Han Solo. Rey is clearly Luke, but she has no suave, competent counterpart. She's basically Batman with a bunch incompetent people around her who seem to pull it off in the end, miraculously, when they all seem like they would quickly end up space dust.

Another reason there is no tension with the characters is they're all awesome at whatever they do. They all just happen to be rockstar pilots even though Finn and Rose are basically the baristas of their fleets, and Rey grew up on a desert planet with barely two coins to rub together. Between starving and being a Jedi, when did she go to flight school? Also, everything's too convenient which reminded me of Independence Day. "Oh, we're locked in jail. No problem, the biggest thief in the universe happens to be locked up with us. Why didn't he escape long ago if he's so good? Who knows, but we sure did luck out!" "Oh no, Princess Leia just got blown into space. Don't worry, she's inherited some Harry Potter magic and will float back to safety."

One thing that stood out that I thought was weird, that Disney would OK an anti-capitalist theme when Disney has a reputation for being one of the more capitalistic/corporate studios, and much more likely to squeeze or strangle the little guy while the execs give themselves 30 million dollar bonuses. Disney isn't at all evil but they run themselves much more like the Republic. A fun studio to work at but not the most fair and you definitely notice a dividing line between the execs and the meager high-skilled workers.

Really, I could go on and on about the problems and plot holes in this film, but, I'm sure I'd just be repeating what others have said. Things I liked about the movie was the two-second appearances of Michaela Coel and Billie Lourde, Laura Dern's small role which was weakened by her acting like a mom, the appearance of Luke and Chewie, even though Luke's character was a weird, curmudgeon hermit. Unlike a lot of reviewers, I liked the humor. I also liked the cute penguin things, which, I hated Jar Jar and wasn't a huge fan of the Ewoks, so, maybe I've softened.

To be honest, I don't know if I'll see the next one. Maybe let's pretend everyone in Rogue One wasn't obliterated and we can just continue with those characters.

title: "The Last Jedi": Flawed Greatness
review:
First off: SPOILER ALERT!

Now, let me begin my review with the positive: I loved this film. Yes, upon first viewing I was so taken back by unexpected moments and emotion that once the credits finished, I was nearly unable to speak. And despite planning on going again later that night (we attended a 7pm preview night screening), I knew my brain needed a good 12 hours to process and think about what I saw before even thinking about going again.

This film has ALL the tropes and makings of a fantastic chapter in the STAR WARS saga: wonderful acting, endearing characters (including the return of "new" favorites and the closing chapters of some of our "old" favorites), an incredible score by John Williams (possibly his third-best in the entire eight-chapter story thus far), and the usual amazing special effects.

The film features just as many dark, unexpected moments as the best of the series (EMPIRE), and literally left my jaw hanging open on multiple occasions- during which I was unable to breathe, move, or do anything but stare wide-eyed at the story unfolding on the screen.

This Episode does our beloved characters justice, introduces new elements of the Force and expands on the preceding mythology ( I do NOT understand those saying this movie abandons everything that came before), offers some beautiful symbolism and lessons regarding OUR own world, and attempts to teach us a very valuable lesson about life (which basically amounts to the ultimate mantra of the Force)- something they've touched on since Episode I and a concept that ALL humans would be wise to learn: let go of the past and do not let it define you and color your world. Accept the past, move beyond it, and evolve as you do.

Now...that said: on with the negative. Specifically: I DO NOT understand all the hate this film is engendering, but, I'll attempt to address some of the complaints I've seen time and again.

First off: the fate of Snoke. WHY is it so hard for people to accept the fate of Snoke? They complain "We didn't learn anything about him!" And? Who cares? We knew what we needed to know in order for the stories of VII and VIII to work. Nothing more, nothing less. Before "Episodes I-III", we basically knew nothing of REAL substance about the Emperor. Yet people seemed content to let the story of the original trilogy work and hinge on HIS evil. Why should this new trilogy be any different in regards to Snoke?

As far as Luke: why is it hard to believe that Luke would follow in the steps of his predecessors (Yoda and Obi-Wan) and hide from his imminent destruction and the dark forces hunting him? He did nothing different than Yoda or Obi-Wan did in choosing to escape near-certain death. The filmmakers absolutely treated his character with the reverence and justice he deserved. After his conversation with Yoda and coming to grips with the TRUE lesson (that apprentices must learn from their Masters' failures and grow beyond what their Masters were and are) of the Force and Jedi, Luke went out on his OWN terms- he became one with the Force after delivering the ultimate sacrifice. And, in doing so, the filmmakers merged Luke's character and action with the icons of our greatest mythologies and religions in our time: he gave up his own existence on the material plane of life in order that his friends, family, and the Rebellion continue to live, exist, and thrive. How is that anything less than the purest, most unselfish sacrifice a human being could ever make?

Next: the "Skywalking" sequence. Why is it so difficult to buy into? Why do some have such troubles accepting the notion that Leia might be just as powerful with the Force as Luke...but with an untapped side? Were these elements truly that difficult to believe? Some say the visual of her floating in space is comedic. Any more so than any of the more far-fetched visuals from previous Episodes? In my opinion, absolutely not.

Is the film perfect? Absolutely not. But NONE of the Episodes are. They all feature plot holes big enough to fly a Corellian space freighter through. Even my favorites from the series have their own glaring flaws.

Yes, the story was, at times, disjointed and the screenplay surely could've benefitted from one more polish (perhaps from Kasdan?). But the editing (especially the seaming of visual matches- compositionally speaking -from one cut to the other) helped bring it all together in a way that I thought worked beautifully.

And, honestly, those saying this is "the worst STAR WARS ever": the filmmaking on display, the storyline, the writing, the score, and the acting are, in my opinion, some of the best in the entire saga. And even if you don't agree...how can you REALLY say it's worse than any of the prequels or even "Jedi", for that matter?

I suspect many of the negative reviews say more about the person critiquing the film than the actual film itself. This film features powerful women who are standing up, acting, and leading in the place of men who simply refuse to make the right choice for the world they live in. Guess what? It happens every day. Every. Single. Day.

That's not to say men can't actually lead...but they CAN grow by taking a step back and sometimes realizing that theirs is not the only voice. And every important male character in this film does just that: Finn, Poe, and, most importantly, Luke.

By facing a "certain point of view" offered to them by their female counterparts, these men grow into the leaders, heroes, and icons they always had the potential to become.

So Luke doesn't ride into battle and save the day in the way you expected. He does so in another, brilliantly-executed way that harkens back to some of the greatest showdowns in Asian (specifically Samurai) cinema.

So no one comes right out and says, "I have a very bad feeling about this." Is it that difficult to imagine that BB-8 does JUST that...in the very opening of the film? Leia herself echoes the sentiment on the comm with Poe. Use your imagination and...your beloved line is there. Just not in the way you imagined.

So they are closing the chapter of old heroes to move into new ones. The simple fact is...STAR WARS is moving on. It belongs to a new generation now. They're closing the book on OUR generation. Is it THAT hard to say goodbye? If so: you're missing the entire point of not only the film...but the teachings of the greatest Jedi himself: Yoda. Learn to accept the past and move on. Let go. Only then can you truly become what you are destined to be...by leaving the old guard behind.

NO ONE is saying that in order to move on to the future you must "DESTROY" the past. If someone is saying that is the case, they're simply NOT paying attention. Kylo Ren mistakes the true wisdom of the Force in that manner. Yoda teaches the truth meaning: you don't DESTROY the past... But you do learn to accept it, you LEARN from it, and you move on.

And that's the key: you move on. You say goodbye.

It hasn't been that difficult for me to say goodbye to Luke, Leia, and others. Sure, Han's death hurt, but that's because Ford means more to me than simply being "just another actor". And, yes, it hurt to see Luke fade out of one plane of being and pass/enter into another. But I understand: it's time.

I adored this chapter in the saga, would readily place it just below V, IV, and VII, and can happily and confidently say: bring on the final episode of the Skywalker saga.

Abrams would be the best to lead that trilogy although The Force Awakens was weak.

title: Ambivalent Reaction to One of My Favorite Director's Foray Into the Star Wars Universe
review:
I waited until after my second viewing and I had some time to fully digest the movie before penning my thoughts. These are not all of my opinions on the film, just the highlights.

This film is dense and as much as I appreciate its depth, it is also its weakness. There was so much to address that often it seemed to skim the surface of what was presented and give the impression there was a lack of focus. The themes of "when darkness rises, the light rises to meet it" and "that things don't turn out the way you think they will" were very present in this film. I found it fresh and disappointing in the same measure. Where JJ was careful not to stomp on the additional lore that Lucas presented in the prequels, Rian had no issues blowing it all up. Cinematically introducing something the TV show has been perpetuating for a while and that Rogue One alluded to, that of the "Grey Jedi". The ancient Jedi philosophy that embraced the Force as a whole, light and dark, not just either side. The belief that the Force is a mystically power that belongs to no one. I can understand why this would be important from a dramatic perspective. Heroes and villains that are internally conflicted are much more three dimensional and interesting than cut out ones.

This is fresh and welcome and in keeping with the meaning of the words "balance in the Force" that Lucas used like confetti throughout the prequels to confusing affect. How is only one side of the Force, balanced? Rian articulated that it was vanity and arrogance that brought down the Jedi order and it was Luke's own vanity that brought down the new Jedi order that he was trying to create.

I am not sure who decided that female Generals would be wearing gowns during a battle, but that was very odd to me. Then add the space walk in said gown, which made for a very campy and bizarre scene in the film.

The producers still have an issue with Rey being seen as a Mary Sue. Someone with Dues Ex Machina abilities that have not really been explained. I kept hoping to see a scene where she does something Mary Sue and another character questions her on it. Then she would reveal that it was her intuition that lead her to do what she did. She doesn't think, she acts on it and it is usually the right thing to do. This would establish that the Force is guiding her to do things she doesn't understand, but invariably work out. I have yet to see that moment in this trilogy.

An ambivalent moment for me came when Rey's parentage was revealed. I hoped for a pedigree lineage, but came to appreciate the everyman heritage. The reinforced idea that anyone can be a powerful Force user. A friend pointed out that the most powerful Jedi seem to come from nothing; Anakin and now Rey. The slap stick humor was a bit over the top to the opposite effect. The principle of diminishing returns comes to mind. This became very evident when Luke milks the sea creatures. That for me was a" jump the shark" moment for the humor. This was a bit surprising considering Mr. Johnson's humor is typically often witty and suitable to the scene. Whereas most of the comedy worked, some scenes fell completely flat.

I don't believe Poe's transformation from a hot shot pilot to an actual forward thinking commander was handled very well. There were no real consequences to him directly from his forced attack on the dreadnaught. He didn't seem to lose anyone close to him or really see the full extent of his actions. Had there been a moment were one of the Resistance allies had signaled back that they weren't coming because they heard of the attack on the dreadnaught and felt that they couldn't trust the Resistance leadership to be good stewards of the reinforcements, with Poe hearing that response. Then he would see the consequences of his hasty actions with total clarity. The believable catalyst for a transformation was missing.

The Finn and Rose adventure struck me as a bit long for its purpose. Some of that time could have been better spent fleshing out other parts of this dense story.

How Luke's story was handled has been my biggest disagreement with this film. I can see Luke losing his confidence as a teacher and even a Jedi after the destruction of his academy, but for him to lose his religion was a step too far. He had seen and done too much to lose his faith in the Force. All of what transpired between he and Rey could have been accomplished without him losing his religion. He could have cut himself off from the Force or stopped reaching out into the galaxy to ensure his location remained hidden from the Knights of Ren. So he could live out his days in his own little pity party island resort.

Some may disagree, but I really enjoyed the final confrontation between Luke and Ren. Just like Ben Kenobi and Darth Vader, the teacher faces the student. Rian established that Force powers can be projected across the galaxy, first by Snoke, then by Luke in dramatic fashion and as he predicted to Rey, it killed him. I saw the final scene, when Ren realized what his former teacher actually was, as a nod back to the moment when Ben Kenobi told Vader that "If you strike me down, I will become more powerful than you can ever imagine". All the visual clues were right in front of us. Luke looked as young as he was when everyone last saw him and he had his father's sabre. Ren never struck him once until Luke wanted him too and the reveal was made. This series is all about Rey and Ren, not the old guard. This film passed the baton to the next generation as it should have. Though I no doubt we'll see Luke again as a Force ghost mentor to Rey in the next film.

Overall, this film was enjoyable. Not what I expected, however that was by design. The Luke story was my biggest disappointment in terms of him losing his religion. It was far out of character for this to happen regardless of whatever plot device it was intended to be, it rang out as false. I didn't expect any of the original cast to survive to the end of Ep 9 and believed like many that Leia was toast when her bridge was destroyed. However, Rian gave us many surprises in this episode and I'm sure it left JJ working hard to find ways to tie up the loose ends Mr. Johnson has now created.

I look forward to seeing how they are tied up in a couple of years.

title: Worse than the Phantom Menace
review:
I had been looking forward to this for some time and I was hoping that at least some of the answers to the questions raised in The Force Awakens would be answered in this instalment. Fans had been speculating for months about the plot of this film and unfortunately far from what was expected. I will go through the problems with this film.

1. It does not take itself seriously: A plot that does not take itself seriously is not believable and therefore we cannot escape into the universe of the film, that was true with this movie, with misplaced humour and mocking tenants of the Jedi faith which were once held sacred, such as when Yoda destroys the sacred texts, makes me believe that Rian Johnson is deliberately trying to destroy the very foundations of the Star Wars story. I have made this criticism about Dr Who ever since Stephen Moffat took over, it has failed to take itself seriously and therefore failed as a TV show, the same is true with Rian Johnsons star wars. At least in the Phantom Menace the Jedi mythology was taken seriously.

2. Luke is a miserable old man: Mark Hamill was right to criticise the direction Luke Skywalker has been taken by this film. Luke has just given up, he is not hiding in the hope of training new jedi to right passed wrongs, instead he just wants to die and initially refuses to train Rey. He was also considering murdering his nephew because he sensed some darkness in him despite having successfully redeemed Darth Vader from the dark side in Return of the Jedi. The character of Luke in the original trilogy was someone who would not give up and sulk away in the way this Luke has.

3. Snoke is wasted potential: As a fan I am downright angry at Rian Johnson for essentially saying that one of the best characters from The Force Awakens (and a Character whose identity has been speculated on for the past two years) doesn't matter. Killing him without any indication of who he is or what motivates him is downright insulting to fans and this was a calculated attempt at fan disservice. I hope he comes back in Episode IX as surely someone as powerful as Snoke has been made out to be cannot die so easily.

4. Rose is the new Jar Jar Binks: When I saw Rose turn up I hoped she would only be in the film for a few minutes and then get back to whatever it was she was doing, instead we have to watch this uninteresting and annoying character for about an hour and a half. She does very little other than get in the way and prevent Finn from making a noble self sacrifice which would have been a fitting end for his character as there is nowhere left to take him at this point.

5. Why didn't Admiral Holdo tell Poe the plan: After General Leia is injured Admiral Holdo takes command of the resistance fleet. There is tension between her and Poe which at first I found quite interesting as I thought she might be a first order spy trying to sabotage them, Poe then stages a mutiny which fails and Leia tells him that they plan to retreat to the planet Kryat, this has the effect of rendering the whole mutiny subplot pointless and cringeworthy, if Holdo just told him the plan there would have been no point to this sub plot.

6. They should have killed Leia: There were two very good moments where they could have killed Leia, the first was when the bridge of the command ship was blown into space, the second was when one person had to stay behind when all the shuttles were launched it should have been Leia and she should have been the one to pilot the command ship into the first order fleet, that would have been a brilliant send off. Due to the passing of Carrie Fisher Leia will now have to be killed off screen.

7. The casino planet sub plot: I did not find this as bad as some other people have but I do feel it was pointless filler content.

8: Where was Anakin Skywalkers ghost: I had heard rumours that Hayden Christensen was on set filming scenes and so I had hoped that Anakin's ghost would appear but he didn't. It would have been good to see how Luke would interact with his father after Return of the Jedi but I guess we won't see that.

9: Why does Luke's projection use the blue lightsaber: I was hoping to see Luke use his ROTJ green lightsaber, instead he uses the blue one which Kylo Ren and Rey had just destroyed, this makes no sense whatsoever. Why didn't Kylo sense something was wrong since he had just snapped that lightsaber in half. It seems very strange to me.

10: Why does Luke die: There really is no need for Luke to die at the end. I didn't think him projecting himself was as bad as many fans think but I would assume the whole purpose of him doing so was so he would not die but if he dies anyway then it's pointless.

11. the grey Jedi. I expected Luke to become a grey Jedi as in someone who makes use of both light and dark in balance with each other, thus fulfilling the idea of bringing balance to the force, I thought the books which turned out to be the jedi sacred texts were in fact the journals of the whills, the whills being force users who can balance both light and dark. This would have been a great direction to take the franchise in and it would have got more people interested for the next film, however they failed to do this and I don't really care about what happens in the next film. I have completely lost interest in the future of this trilogy.

Good parts about the film: I give this film four stars as it explores the relationship between Rey and Kylo Ren very well. Kylo Ren is by far the most interesting character in the movie and his conflict between the light and the dark is explored. Rey's parents being nobody's is quite good as it shows the force is not hereditary.

Conclusion: Rian Johnson should not be allowed to direct any more Star Wars films, the new Trilogy has potential but it needs someone else at the helm. I would not even be against the idea of George Lucas coming back as this film shows that it's better the devil you know than the devil you don't and the prequels are a masterpiece compared to this
