title: Can we pretend this never happened?
review:
There are slivers of goodness in Rian Johnson's The Last Jedi, far outweighed by the film's flaws. The film looks great and some of Johnson's stylistic choices do pay off; one particular showdown towards the end of the film looks like it could have been directed by John Ford or Sergio Leone. Mark Hamill, Daisy Ridley and Adam Driver also give standout performances. Hamill expressed some skepticism (for good reason) regarding the direction of his character, but he seems to have committed himself to the project regardless.

The bane of The Last Jedi is the script. For a running time for two and half hours, so much of what happens in the earlier acts is rendered useless by end of the film. What's worse is that so many of the questioned raised from The Force Awakens are squandered. Much is done at the expense of the Original Trilogy, also cheapening those films in the process. Scattered along the way are ill-placed jokes and political overtones. Johnson is the primary writer credited, so he deserves blame here.

Perhaps the only way to rectify the mess created here is to start Episode IX with the familiar shot of Rey handing Luke Skywalker his old lightsaber. From there we should continue on as if The Last Jedi was nothing but a bad dream.

title: While the Star Wars saga has certainly seen worse films, The Last Jedi is not one to be proud of.
review:
Oof.

As someone who grew up on Star Wars movies, it hurts to watch one that I think is truly bad. These new movies were supposed to bring balance to a damaged franchise but have so far done a shaky job of that.

The Resistance is in a particularly poor state. Led by General Leia Organa (Carrie Fisher) and Vice Admiral Holdo (Laura Dern), the small fleet of Resistance fighters must come up with a plan to escape the First Order's fighters. Meanwhile, as Rey (Daisy Ridley) attempts to train with Luke Skywalker (Mark Hamill), she finds herself strangely connected to Kylo Ren (Adam Driver) and possibly to the dark side of the Force.

This is a sloppy movie, and to its detriment, it has populated its messy plot with mostly uninteresting or unimportant people. It is not, however, without its strengths. As with The Force Awakens, Kylo Ren is the most interesting character in this film and the only one that I have thought much about since seeing it. I find his inner conflict genuinely compelling, and given his personality and past and what he does in this movie, I honestly have no idea where his arc as a character will go. He even has a uniquely brutish and aggressive fighting style that makes his lightsaber work genuinely intimidating. The movie has me engaged just about any time he is on screen, and as he interacts with Rey, it becomes apparent that the two of them are just about the only emotionally engaging parts of the movie. I have remained interested in Rey's journey since The Force Awakens, and while I am confident she will find her place on the right side of history, just how she gets there is likely to be interesting to watch.

I honestly cannot say much about the rest of the cast, as neither the returning characters nor the new ones are particularly interesting. I would like to speak highly of Mark Hamill's return to the role of Luke Skywalker, but to my disappointment, the script hands him some interesting dialogue and ideas, juggles them a bit, and then walks off in boredom. He is an important part of Rey's personal journey but does not in my opinion present much compelling material to the audience aside from his vague distaste toward the Jedi. Otherwise, the cast is almost completely forgettable: Poe Dameron is unlikably rash, Leia is just sort of there, Finn is the same as before, and Vice Admiral Holdo would be more at home in a PTA meeting than in a respected military position.

These characters spend most of the film standing and talking - sometimes walking and talking - about hope and about how poorly The Resistance is doing. A convoluted mashup of subplots arises and ultimately leads nowhere, and, well, the bad guys are bad. The Last Jedi's primary flaw is in just how pointless most of the film is, and after I finished watching it, I had a tough time remembering the majority of it aside from the finale. In that way, this movie reminds me of Rogue One with its structural issues and epic finale. Despite its many flaws, that film was at least fairly straightforward in delivering its simple plot.

I have other, smaller nitpicks with the film. For example, I think that the humor is often arbitrary, unfunny, and out of place. There are several clumsy comic relief moments and important scenes interrupted by these jokes. This is a trend that I have noticed in several Disney-owned films recently, particularly Spider-Man Homecoming from earlier this year, and as I commented in that review, it comes across as the filmmakers being afraid to look genuine and make the audience feel too much emotionally. Also, Daisy Ridley is a poor fighter, and her couple of fight scenes look more like dress rehearsal footage than the epic Star Wars fights of other films. I hope she trains a bit more for Episode IX. Finally, there are multiple points in the film where the script seems to subvert audience expectations entirely for the sake of subversion. There is, of course, nothing wrong with taking material in unexpected directions, but in this case it harms the overall experience of this film and feels like the movie wants to be recognized for innovation over its ability to tell a story.

Overall, The Last Jedi feels like a rough draft. With its cobbled-together opening, stumbled-through middle act, and effective finale, there is a good movie in here somewhere. That is not what I saw in the theater, though. The Last Jedi has me concerned with the trajectory of these new Star Wars films, as I enjoyed The Force Awakens, thought Rogue One was mediocre, and now find this one to be simply bad. I am still going to watch the next release given my hopeless love for the series, but it will need to deliver in ways that this one did not in order to keep me interested down the road.

title: Adds Up To Far Less Than the Sum of its Parts
review:
My first reaction while watching this film was that the detractors must be wrong. Hamill's acting is very good; the battle scenes have effective moments; I was fine with the level of humor (not particularly funny, but okay). The mystery of why Luke was acting the way he was, seemed like a mystery ... and I was intrigued to know the solution.

But the longer the film drags on, the more it seems that there would be no positive solutions to the any of the mysteries or plot elements it set up. Before I hit the 2 hour mark, I am losing interest and hoping for the film to end. But the film drags on; & each passing minute seems to bang further nails into the coffin of any sense of hope or positive feelings.

Luke (Hamill's character) ends up being one of the most disappointing things about this film, for reasons that are in no way Hamill's fault. Hamill could have brought much to the new trilogy, if used effectively, but not only has that opportunity been wasted, but it has seemingly been wasted with devastating finality.

Some critics have gone on about the film's gender politics. As to that, I will only say only that this might not be the film for young boys, because it offers them nearly nothing in terms of positive male role models. The overall effect matters more than the individual examples. The first and second time Poe Dameron got justly humiliated by the female authority figures, I was okay with it. But the continuing humiliation of Poe detracts not only from Poe, but also from Finn, and even from new spunky female Rose, by rendering their story arcs and their heroic efforts pointless and even counterproductive. Then Finn tries to be heroic in the finale, and Rose puts a stop to that too. Thus does the film seem to cut off its nose to spite its face. All this is part of a broader problem of a confusing array of story elements adding up to little or nothing.

But I suppose, for the girls, there's still Rey to root for. The filmmakers also give us a good look at brooding bad boy Kylo Ren's manly waxed chest, and quite evidently regard this as a treat. Not for me, sorry. I sense where this is going, and I don't find it particularly interesting. It remains to be seen if the new Star Wars will find its new audience; but I can definitely see why so much of the old guard feels let down.

title: "Permission to get in an X-wing and blow something up" -Sums up the movie
review:
Star Wars: The Last Jedi deviates from the homage that was The Force Awakens in narrative and quality. Disney jumped the shark in this disappointing, forced, cartoonish joke. The Force Awakens mashed everything we loved about the originals (albeit, maybe too much) into a modern mix of pop entertainment. The Last Jedi subverts fan expectation in favor of a more logically inept, dramatically empty, and cringeworthy bore.

The Last Jedi surprisingly didn't completely rehash The Empire Strikes Back; it took some risks and delivered a few surprises, but the overall execution was poor. Mark Hamill put in his best performance probably ever. The rest of the cast was fine except for a few distractingly annoying faces (Rose). Rian Johnson brought some humor, self-awareness, and philosophical dialogue surrounding the legend of the Jedi resulting in something new in a Star Wars movie. The storyline of Luke's resentment towards the Jedi and his mysterious past with Kylo Ren was compelling and the only promise the movie had going forward. However, everything quickly fell apart after the first act.

*Spoilers Begin Here* The Last Jedi didn't take itself seriously enough by having just as much comedy and self-referential humor as an SNL sketch. Many of the jokes fell flat and completely killed whatever tension or emotion was already present (Poe's opening prank call, Luke's cheeseball one liners). The action was totally uncompelling and boring (didn't even have a lightsaber fight in a Star Wars movie). Anyone with an arc was unkillable, and the worse thing about it is that they constantly put the characters in absurdly dangerous situations and they pulled through completely unscathed - not due to the power of the mystical force but due to terrible writing. The Leia skywalking space scene is one of the most laughably bad scenes I've seen in a long time. For a second I thought I was watching Mary Poppins. The scene where Rose saves Finn by crashing into his spaceship should've killed them both but due to terrible writing and a lack of testicular fortitude, they both pull through unscathed just so Rose could start a Disneyfied love triangle. The whole Casino sequence with Rose and Finn was way too boring and bloated. The BB-8 controlling the AT-ST to save the day scene had my eyes rolling. What was up with the First Order and their aim trajectory? They couldn't just send in a faster ship to blow the Resistance out of space. And the fan-servicing Yoda scene lost me because Yoda looked so weird. Why couldn't they just use the same puppet?

Rian Johnson took a serious risk during the obligatory confrontational scene - involving Rey, Kylo Ren, and Snoke - when Kylo Ren turns on his Emperor-esque master by using the Force to turn on a lightsaber cutting Snoke's body in half. I'd be lying if I said I saw that coming especially since Disney has one more movie planned in episode IX (and lots more planned after that). After that scene I couldn't help but feel disappointed because Snoke was hyped up in The Force Awakens to be some mysterious force-wielding badass with an interesting backstory. Refusing to develop Snoke and by him dying looking like a total moron was more anticlimactic than ballsy.

Rian Johnson basically said "F U" to JJ Abrams in how he completely strayed away from what was set up in The Force Awakens and by leaving not much left to work with in Episode IX. For instance, he kills off Snoke, leaving the conflicted Kylo Ren as the only villain, kills Luke, likely to come back as a spirit, leaves Leia alive, subjecting everyone to awkward CGI Leia, forces a weird and likely to be cringeworthy love triangle, outrages fans over the stupidity of this movie, and worst of all, probably alienated many Star Wars fans leaving them with nothing but a vengeful demand for the end of Star Wars.

title: A disaster
review:
I made this account purely so that I could rant about how frustrated I am about the film. Having been excited about it for the past year and a bit and after trying my best to avoid all spoilers, I left the cinema feeling nothing less than devastated at the direction Star Wars is being taken. I saw the film 2 additional times just to be sure and with each time I left feeling more disgusted than the last. Lets take a brief look at my major disagreements without even considering Luke and his *new* character.

  • A Mary Sue protagonist who, with 2 days of 'Jedi training' is able to defeat the First Order's most powerful soldiers and is able to match that of Kylo Ren, a descendant of Anakin who was trained by both Jedi and Sith. This throws everything from the past movies and EU out of the window; you no longer need years of extensive training to be able to accurately wield and control the force nor do you need any training with a lightsaber to be able to use one.


  • Rose (ugh) and Finn go off to some casino planet to find a master code breaker. Even if you ignore the political undertones, they get thrown in jail for a PARKING violation and they just so happen to find exactly who they're looking for in their cell. This turns out to be a completely unnecessary exercise for two reasons; they get captured anyway AND had purple hair lady merely told everybody her plan, going to the lead Star Destroyer would have evidently been pointless.


  • 'The' Leia scene was indescribably horrible.


  • Opening scenes with the Dreadnaught; most of the incredibly slow and large bombers are wiped out immediately for obvious reasons. Cliche plot armour is placed on the remaining bomber who, after somehow surviving tie fighters who for some reason didn't shoot them down, is able to destroy one of the First Order's most dangerous and large ships with one payload.


  • Vice Admiral Purple Hair (her character was so disconnected with me as a viewer that I just don't care to even look her name up) has a plan but for the entire movie refuses to tell anybody about it whilst their support ships one by one are destroyed for more or less no reason. This carries on for so long that a mutiny occurs.


  • Admiral Akbar, a fan favourite, is merely thrown in the trash. Why not have him become commander and send him off in a memorable way?


  • Snoke, who had been established as this incredibly powerful, almost godlike, force user who despite being able to use the force merely via hologram died because his puerperal vision was't quite wide enough. He was also given no back story as to who he was, where he came from OR his objectives.


  • The First Order is this incredibly powerful government who 'reigns' over the galaxy. Despite this, they only have about 3 ships to go after the remaining resistance forces who, once destroyed, would allow them to rule unopposed. In any case, they merely follow them in a slower ship shooting at them over the course of 18 or so hours rather than cutting them off with another ship or signaling for reinforcements.


  • After Rose saves Finn, Rose is somehow dragged back into the Rebel base across what is likely to be many kilometers of open ground. They somehow do this despite being in clear sight of the AT-M6s and AT-ATs.


  • Forced humour that not only fails to connect but takes the audience out of an otherwise tense scene.


The only thing stopping this from being a 1 is the visual effects and a degree of empathy for the actors. Kudos to you for doing your best with what you were given. I fear the Johnson's trilogy where everybody can use the force and control it with no training at all. Absolutely disappointing.

title: The Desecration of Star Wars: Episode 2.
review:
Luke: From hero to zero. After bringing hope to the Galaxy, ending the Empire, and bringing Vader back to the Light, Luke now mopes around on an island like a drunkard due to drinking too much alien boob milk. He's doing absolutely nothing. Wasted opportunity. His character devolves into one that disrespects the Jedi and he desecrates the original teachings along with a catatonic puppet Yoda ghost (even though they had years to do so before Rey showed up, and force Ghosts might as well just shoot lighting bolts at Snoke if they can influence physical reality all along). All while, Han's death does not sway Luke to rejoin the Resistance, nor the impending death of his sister and comrades still carrying the flag of hope he once crafted. His lessons half fast and the reasons were that Rey was gifted in the Force, since the Force belongs to all things like some social justice motive that the Jedi order have hogged it all to themselves over the millennia and now the Force must be allowed for embrace by all people. Hogwash.

Rey: Absolutely no development for her character in the movie. We learn she was jettisoned by her junkie parents and she's nothing special - other than having supreme knowledge of the force. Yeah that's really interesting....the hidden message here is that the Force is for all people, not just for the Jedi and Sith. You don't have to be anything special. You can wake up and move boulders with your mind one day!

Snoke: Absolutely no revelations about him, despite leading audiences for the last 2 years with theories and discourse. Fans may never know his true origins unless it is addressed in the next installment. But it doesn't matter now, as his anticlimactic departure ensured any involvement of him in future events would be inconsequential. Great!

First Order: The first order is no longer menacing. The supreme leader who held such conviction is now gone. Phasma was defeated by Fin who is not endowed with any special skills as a former Storm Trooper (he also doesn't hesitate to kill Storm Troopers now when in the last movie he was conflicted). General Hux or "Junior" gets punched around and is no longer taken seriously. The First Order's crafted ships cannot take down a simple cruiser in a slow speed chase despite in the past showing military dominance and weapon supremacy. Kylo Ren is still conflicted and not a threatening leader as he was alluded to in the flashbacks involving the the Knights of Ren (who have disappeared too because why not!). The First Order might as well be a loosely organized extremist group led by children since all major players are gone.

Rose and DJ: Their inclusion in the events had no reason other than to diversify the cast and appease global audiences. I mean, I am not against diversity, but you can't just create new characters and throw them into a subplot with no payoff. The scenes at the Casino to save donkey dogs from captivity and recruit DJ who grumbled all his lines - was all pointless. It was boring 30 minutes I thought I would walk out of the theater and get popcorn. The kiss at the end between Fin and Rose was also awkward as they had no chemistry throughout the film. In fact, Fin and Rey had more chemistry but they do not even contact each other for the whole film, and Fin literally mentally writes her off without a care of her well being. That inconsistency in character relationships is a whole other issue. Rose's comments about capitalism at the end of the Casino scene and saving animals was also social justice warrior crap shots.

CGI: CGI was bad. I am not sure, but the film had a grainy look to it and the dark scenes with heavy shadows were barely noticeable. The cruisers and ships also looked like they were filmed in front of a green screen using poorly detailed models and had no fluidity in their movement.

Leia: She does not bear any respect as a General and is instead seen as Mother Goose for the Resistance. They made her look tired and she walks around almost defeated in every scene. They made her lack any leadership other than being some overseer while she hobbles depressed in the shadows. This is not the Leia we remember.

Entertainment: The film was not fun to watch. Even the prequel trilogy had life, great action, plenty of colorful locations, interesting characters, and an expansive universe. This movie literally takes place in probably 4 locations: ship interiors, some red salty planet mirroring Hoth, space, and a Casino planet. Wow what adventure!

Star Wars Ended after episode 6 in my eyes. Literally I would pretend there are no more Star War Movies after episode 6. Even through episode 7 was decent, it has retcon by this mess and no longer relevant for viewing.

title: Annoying characters - who cares?
review:
TLJ has been thoroughly examined by others, but I wanted to expand on what I see as the main problem.

Star Wars was never about the story; it's a cliched one after all. The plot could be set against prehistoric, Roman, medieval, western, modern, future times in any language and culture and still work.

To me, it was always about the characters: Luke, Han and Leia. They were easy to identify with and root for. They were people you'd want to be or at least hang out with.

The problem with the new trilogy is that all the players are so unlikable, even the old ones like Luke. I lost interest in the outcome of the struggle because I didn't care whether the good guys won or not.

I could have overlooked all the gaping plot holes if there were one character I cared about but there were none.

title: Subverting expectations should not be the end goal of a director.
review:
I happen to find all the characters in this new trilogy to be charismatic and enjoyable. Is Rey a Mary Sue? Yep. Best pilot, best mechanic, beats Kylo with no training, beats jedi master Luke with no training, everybody loves her, has no real conflicts or weaknesses, to overcome, etc. I like her anyway, just based on personal charisma. Was Snokes an abortion of a character/plotline? Yep. Mysteriously powerful figure, introduced in Force Awakens, was summarily deleted without any exploration of his nature. I guess I'm ok with that, since his CGI was really bad. I can also deal with Kylo being the big bad from here on out, since he's more interesting, except he isn't overwhelming in power compared to Rey, so it will be hard to make a confrontation scary in the future. 
Supporting characters: Poe, Fin, Rose, should be allowed to be heroes, not made to seem foolish. Poe is supposed to learn a lesson to "trust your leaders" apparently, which is WAY out of line with the Star Wars ethos. And if you're going to do that, you'd better be damned sure the plot makes sense, which it doesn't. Admiral Holdo (military typically wear uniforms by the way, not slinky evening dresses and purple hair) had a plan she wouldn't share...then when she shared it, it was absurd. The whole "They won't track us if we're in lifeships" plan was just a retarded concept. Why would the audience think that was a thing? They were in visual range for gods sake, let alone sensor range. The questions pile up: Why does she self sacrifice when ships have autopilot? Why not have fleet all scatter into hyperspace since only one enemy ship has the tracking device? Why not use one ship to destroy the rest of fleet if hyperspace collisions are so effective? Why was Poe demoted for using the death of 20 soldiers to destroy around a million 1st order soldiers and a dreadnaught? It was seen as a loss when the "leadership" were sacrificing ships left and right for no goddamned reason? Since when do these ships run out of fuel? Never happened before in all the other episodes...never a concept. The hacker character betrays them for, I'm led to believe, enormous sums of money, for revealing the plot to destroy the tracker and telling them to "look out the goddamned window because they've got this really clever plan to leave by lifeboat. You should blow those lifeboats up." And do they really just reward escaped thieves with enormous sums of money when they could just shoot him? All these flawed and illogical story mechanisms are to what? Show the folly of 'seat of the pants' heroism the supporting cast were engaged in? Why is THAT a lesson we want our characters learning in the frickin' Star Wars universe? Are they going to peacefully negotiate and follow orders in the next installment? Sounds like a hoot.
Now granted, the whole franchise is not all that logical a 'verse, but it has its own internal messed up rules and logic that we've come to accept. When you break the internal rules and formulas, you draw attention to these flaws and pull the viewer out of the story. Bad idea in other words.
Final and most critical beef is Luke Skywalker: Ok, the guy's bitter and disillusioned. That's ok for a starting point. Gives the possibility for a character arc where he ends up someplace else. Well, it was a damned short arc. Went from "Jedi must end and I don't want to help anyone" to I'm going to use this power nobody ever heard of and go quietly "poof" in a way nobody anticipated after an anticlimactic battle scene that really accomplished nothing. The delay he was supposed to be providing? Wasn't necessary. The resistance left AFTER the cannon went off and destroyed the door anyway. Luke's death was such a missed opportunity to move the emotional needle of the audience, but I don't think anybody even welled up. We did't have time to realize he was even in peril. Nobody was there to witness him go "poof" and cry "NO!". Whether the power or the scene made sense or not, is the lesser sin here. There shouldn't have been a dry eye in the house and they'll never have that opportunity again. Anyone who liked this movie had no real connection to the old characters in my opinion, and had no expectations of it other than as an amusement park ride, which it did deliver, hence my 3 star rating.

title: Gutted
review:
The Last Jedi was a great disappointment to me. In fact I am creating my 1st IMDB account just so I can express some of my thoughts and hopefully stop being bothered about this movie. I really wanted to like this movie and it has some of my favorite scenes in a star wars movie. That said here is my short review.

For some background on myself I am not old enough to have seen all the original trilogy in theaters but I did see Return of the Jedi in the theater. In fact it is one of the most vivid memories of my young childhood. So these films had a big impact on my childhood. In fact i don't really remember a time where start wares was not a part of my life. I While there are many critiques of some of the issues with this movie I will focus on a few that really ruined it for me. The 1st and biggest for me is the portrayal of Luke. in this move we are supposed to believe that Luke just gave up and went to some island to die because Ben Solo started to turn to the Dark Side. This basically undoes all character progression we see for Luke in episodes 4-6. This was just a leap to far for me and really pulled me out of the movie. i probably could have gone along with this plot point if they had spent some time developing this point. Instead all we got to support this was a few short flashbacks and some very short exposition. Maybe they could have cut the pointless Canto Bight stuff and spent some time here). One possible way this could have been down would be if Luke had been married and Ben Solo killed his spouse. I probably would not have liked this but I could have gone along with it. Many people have said there is precedent for Luke going into exile because both Yoda and Obi Wan did the same. I don't buy this. In this film Luke just gives up and goes into exile to die. Obi Wan went to Tatooine to watch over Luke and try and make sure Vader/Palpatine didn't find Luke. Yoda went to Dagoba to bide his time and see if there might come a way to undo what had been done. From my perspective they both still carried a spark of hope. Luke just gave up with little explanation as to why. Are you freaking kidding me!?!? The next point I will talk about is the overall tone of the movie. The writer seemed to go out of his way to make sure we knew the that all the stuff from episodes 1-7 does not matter from this point on. There were some serious nihilistic undercurrents here. He went out of his way to say it doesn't matter who Snoke is. It doesn't matter who Rey's parents are. The Jedi origins and history don't matter. By the end of the movie the resistance is basically decimated with 1 ship and about 20 people surviving. I get that Disney probably wants to reset things so they can take the series in some different directions but did they have to go out of there way to tear down just about everything that came before to do it? I really wish they would have finished out episodes 8 and 9 before trying to reset everything.

If episodes 4-6 were about hope and optimism then 8 seem to be about failure and deconstruction. Some have drawn parallels between this and Empire Strike Back because of some of the darker themes. These 2 movies do have some similarities. At the end of ESB the rebels suffered some severe setbacks and lost the Hoth base, there was still a fleet and a sense that things could turn around. At the end of the last Jedi there is basically nothing but Poe, Fin, Chewie, Rey, the droids and the Falcon with a few other random people. This leaves me scratching my head as to where the story goes from here and I am not really interested in where this story leads. The last point I will make is that the writer/director seemed to go out of his way to subvert every expectation. While I like some surprises i wish they were tied to a better story. I couldn't escape the feeling that I was being trolled throughout this movie. You expect to find out about Rey's past? Nope!. You expect to find out how the first order came to be? nope! you expect to find out more about Snoke? Nope You expect Admiral Holdo to act rationally and explain the plan so people know they are not just waiting for a slow death? Nope. Who are the Knights of Ren? Nope! You expect Luke to not be a bitter old man who doesn't care that his sister is in grave danger? Nope! You expect that Finn will retain some of the character growth he had from the last movie? Nope! You expect Finn to go out and sacrifice himself to save what is remaining of his friends? Nope! You expect Poe to not act like a complete ass twice? Nope! You expect this film to make sense given the existing canon? Nope!

It seems like the movie was just one big head fake after another at the expense of making a movie that makes sense in the context of what came before. Its as if the director was so concerned with the criticism that the force awakens was just a retread that they decided to throw everything out the window whether it made sense or not. There were some of these surprises that I liked (especially the throne room fight). But overall I think this movie is a mess that destroys more than it builds. Worst of all the destruction has effectively eradicated my desire to see any more of the Disney Star Wars. I really enjoyed Rogue One and i thought The Force Awakens was ok. I even appreciated some aspects of the prequels. But this one just left me confused and disappointed.

There is a Youtuber named David Stewart who has a few videos breaking down the issues with this movie (in a better fashion than I can). One of the points he made was that this movie has the aesthetic of a Star Wars movie but it does not have the heart of one. There is no heart here just window dressing.

On the one hand, as a fan of big budget spectacle sci-fi adventures movies I was blown away. In that regard the movie delivers. It's exciting and runs at a brisk pace delivering action and peril for its characters in equal measure.
On the other hand, as a Star Wars fan, I was deeply disappointed. After waiting two years since The Force Awakens, and thirty some odd years since The Return of the Jedi, the movie failed to deliver on some key moments we were hoping for.

title: A film desperately trying to be great by being too smart
review:
A quick overview of why it was so bad: *Space "bombers". *Flying through space surrounded by an oxygen bubble. *Poor character development *Overuse of special effects for no effect

One of the first things we see in the move is a space bomber. While this is not the first time that a space bomber has been used in the Star Wars franchise, it is certainly one of the silliest. The Tie Bombers used in Empire Strikes Back seemed to be using some sort of way to propel the bombs out of the bombers and onto the asteroids where the Falcon was hiding. These rebel bombers seemed to actually be relying on gravity to drop, which doesn't seem possible since that Dreadnought is not big enough to have that much gravity. Also, the whole scene with the bomber crew member trying to launch the bombs was a poor excuse for drama. Was she supposed to be unable to climb, so that's why she was madly kicking the ladder or was that just a poor choice of trying to get the bombing trigger?

The whole scene with Leia and the attack on the last big cruiser was working well, right up until Leia was about to die in space. In no way did I want Leia to die, but since the entire bridge of the ship was blown out then so be it. The camera zoomed in on Leia and I thought this is their tribute to Carrie Fisher, giving a long shot and letting us think about it. I actually started to tear up...and then they pull this stupid move worthy of B-movie. Though Leia was just blown out into the vacuum of space, likely should have been killed by the concussive force, she was supposedly total conscious and able to pull a bunch of random oxygen molecules around her to allow her to survive, use the force to pull herself back to the ship, and even though it was not an airlock she was able to get herself back into the ship. I know we're dealing with Science Fiction, but there is still supposed to be something close to science. Even though Star Wars is more quasi-science there should at least be some basic suspension of disbelief and general constraints. If Leia was that powerful, why didn't she just use the Force to bash all the enemy ships together or cause their ordinance to explode in their ships.

For character development, it seems they admire Quentin Tarantino's random plot twists. We figure there is a big story behind Snoke. Maybe there was originally a Snoke story, but instead they just slice him in half and forget about him half way through the movie. Phasma may be a small role, but at least make something more of the role especially when you have a big name like Gwendoline Christie playing her. Unfortunately that was not the case, and she is limited to a fight with Finn and then dropped into a fire. Want to know about Rey's parents? Well they were nothing and we're not going to talk about them. All these seem to be a consistent war on character development in this movie.

Finally, the red sand on the planet just over played. Ultimately, the red sand existed so they could point to Luke and say there were no footprints, so we have proof he wasn't even there. Why? There does not seem to be a reason except to maybe give a little extra CGI work to people. That lightsaber battle could have happened on a solid floor with no evidence that Luke wasn't real, and we could have accept that he still wasn't there. I think the only thing it does prove is that Kylo was to dumb or enraged to realize Luke wasn't there. It didn't do anything for the audience. Even the lame hydrofoil fighters that stirred up the red dirt seemed pointless and dumb.

I prefer to give useful feedback when critiquing but this was one of those instances where things legitimately seemed dumb, pulled right out of the imagination of someone who has no writing experience let alone sci-fi experience. I'm not sure if that is the case with Rian Johnson but it sure seems like it. If Disney is considering giving him script control of some yet-to-be-named Star Wars trilogy, they should think again.

title: Lack of respect for good storytelling
review:
Firstly, I am a 40 year old male, born in the same year as New Hope was released and have been a huge fan of Star Wars since I was old enough to watch it. I am prepared to accept that my review may be biased given my love for the franchise but having had a couple of days to digest my opinion, I have come to the conclusion that my disappointment at this latest effort is not without real justification.
My feeling is that there was a distinct lack of respect in the writing. I don't simply mean in regards to respecting Star Wars lore although that is of course also true, but more to do with established rules of good storytelling.
From the start and throughout, humour was used at hugely inappropriate moments and although in and of themselves, the jokes were well executed, they detracted from nearly all of the more meaningful, darker moments of the film. This served to halt your emotional connection to the scenes and to the characters.
This highlights another flaw with the writing which is character development and consistency. Rey, we are supposed to believe has come from nothing, with no formal training other than being a scrap dealing street (desert) fighter, and yet is a deadly, highly skilled Jedi from the start. It may turn it to be false but revealing her to be no more than a skip rat, descended from skip rats doesn't do much to make her super powers believable. I mean, if you wanted to do the "heroes can come from nothing" thing, then fair enough, but there still has to be a developing arc otherwise all we have is a superhero and we have enough of those films to be getting on with if that's what we're after. These films are always about growth and development through adversity and hard work, discipline and devotion to a cause or spirituality; that being a hero means not having the most power or skill but of doing the right thing.
Similarly, our view of Kylo Ren is simply a test of our trust in what we're told rather than what we're shown. We never saw him with his parents and were never privy to his training or relationship with Luke so to expect us to invest in a sadness or hope for him just based on trust of the writer, is misguided. This is not to say Adam Driver's tearful anguished close ups were badly acted, but given the lack of back story to his or Rey's life, an audience can't be expected to feel how we're being asked to feel. Perhaps this is as much of the fault of J.J. In Force Awakens too for not covering any of it but it wasn't so crucial in that movie as the conflict hadn't grown.
I honestly felt more emotional bond between Rey and Finn when they finally caught up during the rescue in Force Awakens because we'd seen them already develop a relationship and mutual respect, they'd argued and bonded.
This sort of development is vital to how we respond to characters and then to how we respond to the scenarios in which you place these characters. To defy such laws of storytelling isn't brave, it's naive and foolish.
There are character flaws with Finn and Rose's relationship too which lead up to one of the most contradictory morality messages delivered by anyone in the film. Saving him from saving hundreds of his comrades and loved ones just so she could berate him and tell him he should be saving loved ones not fighting the enemy. Was this entire (completely pointless albeit cinematically magnificent) scene written by two different people? Their entire story together was weak and ill-planned and resulted in their efforts being seen to be not only futile but seriously damaging to the resistance. Yoda's message in the film that we grow through failure is one thing, but these two wouldn't be celebrated as heroes upon their return but as defectors and traitors. To simply imply that the few remaining resistance fighters that weren't eliminated as a direct result of these bumbling dimwits would simply say "oops, better luck next time" is again a flaw in the story.
And to return to Yoda - I can live with the summoning of lightening from beyond the grave if I must (and I also appreciate that there is a rumour that Rey has saved the books and taken them aboard the Millennium Falcon) but to have him as far as we and Luke are concerned, burning books as a means of delivering his message says more of our throwaway culture of downloadable content than anything else. "Burn it all because it's what's inside that counts" is a message loaded with a lack of respect for sentiment, for old ways and for at its core, books! which the next generation of Star Wars addicts to whom this film is directed, could well do without.
Perhaps this isn't bad story writing so much. But as the film is clearly loaded with pseudo political messages under the thinly veiled guise of the casino scene with rich people looking down on the poor and profiting from war, messages to our young is evidently on the minds of Hollywood and I know from my memory as a child that the stuff that Yoda says and does will remain longer in a child's mind than some long speech by a pair of numpties staring over a balcony at a horse donky thing. To deliver a subtle message that you can just obliterate history and that it doesn't matter is putting a lot of faith in our disenfranchised youths not to go on to repeat our mistakes.
There has been much written about the false promises and gotcha moments too so I'll do nothing other than agree with them all. It appears that the writer has no idea how to deliver a twist and instead offers a variety of "pranks". Again, poor and naive story writing.
There is much else but I feel it's more my opinion on how I feel characters would have behaved and as that is speculation in a fictional world, it's unfair for me to criticise.
I will however say to all those who believe that many people are moaning simply because it's not true to Star Wars and that they should embrace the new, that this shows a lack of respect to the franchise and to those who have invested in it. If you have so much courage of conviction in your story, write a different film using different characters. To just go blowing up and writing off all the old characters simply to hurry things along so you have carte blanche to do what you will with the new generation of characters is cheating. It's like buying a Ferrari and tearing the bodywork off and putting it onto a VW chassis and still calling it a Ferrari. You have to treat the whole thing with a certain amount of respect otherwise you end up with a different franchise which lacks the solidity which has meant that the Star Wars name has remained in the consciousness of people (not just its fans) for 40 years.
All this said, it is a visually stunning piece. Acting is solid and only suffers through bad story writing and poor direction.
The film will of course go on to make loads of money but I fear that money is being taken from the people who hope to wow their kids with their own memories of the Jedi ways and to pass on the message of hope and heroic deeds going rewarded. Whether this latest trilogy is going to be solid enough a story to have the future generation still talking about it to their kids is still to be seen. I personally have my doubts.

title: Sad to say, this is the worst Star Wars movie ever made.
review:
I've been a Star Wars fan my entire life. I did not like "The Force Awakens" to begin with. It had it's moments but JJ Abrams just didn't seem to be a real fan of the saga. Things like: Stormtrooper now almost equals Sith in fighting skills. Rey more powerful than the villain without zero training. It's not some small things. It just breaks up everything of what made episode 1-6. It doesn't follow how the force works. JJ Abrams, watch "Rogue One" Vader fighting scene. Thats how it works in Star Wars universe. I know Kylo isn't fully trained yet, but it doesn't matter.

It also contains very bad humourous screenplays. Screenplays that have not until now been seen in Star Wars. It feels like "Disney Channel" and in it's worst moments: "Space Balls".

The things that was good with TFA was that it opened up for an exciting follow up. Now a year later, it came. "The Last Jedi".

Instead of using the exciting threads TFA threw up in the air for some smashes for the sequel. The new scriptwriters didn't seem to like them. They put them to the ground and threw them out of the window. For what? Nothing.

"The Last Jedi" is a mess that kills of cool classic characters and replaces them with nothing. It's a shallow story. Why would I like to see episode 9?

Without writing an essay on how bad this was. I hated that: -The strong part of Star Wars has always been the dark threat, where is it now? Weak Kylo? -Who was/is Phasma? (I'm sure she makes a pointless return.) -Who was Snoke? All that CGI for what? -Luke talks about "lasers swords" instead of light sabers. -Mary Poppins. (Carrie Fisher as Leia did an excellent job though.) -Las Vegas in space. Why this subplot? To make a point for the end? Cut it out. -"The Return of the Jedi" scene that almost ends like in "The return of the Jedi". -"Space Balls" scenes. (That beginning. No one laughed in the theatre.) -Luke tosses his fathers old lightsaber over his shoulder like a joke, the one he held when he once lost his hand. OMG scriptwriters! -Kylo is joking with Rey about her parents right? All that build up in TFA for this?

I liked that: -Finn feels more chilled and natural as a character in this one. (He was just out of breath in TFA.) -Purple hair was right and not Poe. (The only working twist in this movie.)

Just a thought...

How cool had it been if Snoke discovers that he took the wrong apprentice in Kylo, learning that Rey is of possession of larger dark side of the force. He uses Kylo to get to Rey and get her to kill Kylo cause he is the lighter and weak one. Now we have a crazy strong villain in Rey. Now that would have been something for episode 9 to continue... I would have seen that movie.

I'm sad to say that "The Last Jedi" was bad for Star Wars franchise. It hurts the saga badly and forever. I wish someone else made this movie.

title: Massive disappointment
review:
Strong acting and stunning visuals are not enough to save this movie from an appallingly bad script and so many inconsistencies introduced to the Star Wars universe.

I can only guess that the people who wrote the script lacked any imagination whatsoever. They also 'broke' the universe in many ways..

  • Chrome armour deflects blaster shots? Why aren't all the troopers wearing this - instant victory!
  • Lightspeed vessels can be used as ramming weapons? The rebels could've used the medical support ship to ram the pursuing destroyer in the first 10 minutes.
  • Force ghosts can manipulate the physical world? Yoda could just kill the bad guys with lightning, etc.
  • It's possible to turn on a light-saber using the Force? Why not turn off you're opponents saber mid battle?


C'mon people, your audience ain't that stupid..

title: Good intro, a middle a little boring, phenomenal ending.
review:
A lot of people REALLY hate this movie, but honestly I really liked it. There were a few things a didn't like, but more things that I did like.

The things I didn't like aren't too bad, but could have been better. The casino scene on Cantonicai is what is getting the most hate, but it wasn't as bad as people say it is. The only problem I had with it is that it dragged on, but the meaning behind it and the new aliens were cool enough to keep my interest. The other thing I didn't like was the Luke, didn't really seem like Luke. Not the entire performance, but just random things that he did in the movie seemed like something Mark Hamill would do, but not Luke Skywalker. Other than that and the scene with Leia floating to the bridge, I don't have any problems with the movie besides small nitpicks. Okay now the stuff I liked. The effects where awesome and have noticeably improved. A lot of people has problems with the plot not revealing some of the mysteries of the last movie, but I didn't have any problems with it. Killing off Snoke got a lot of people mad, (debunking the theories and all that) but the story wasn't really about him, I honestly just thought that was a problem with The Force Awakens making him all mysterious and then just killing him. Another thing that people didn't like was the humor. I thought the humor was funny, only a few jokes didn't really pass.

In the end this was a really strong movie with some problems, but it made up for that with the acting, plot, effects, and characters.

(ps this is obviously very biased)

title: Great movie if you are a new fan of Star Wars
review:
Spoilers ahead..

I am of the generation that was a kid when Star Wars first came out. As such, this was the movie franchise that I have the strongest emotional ties to.

The new movies are entertaining. The last Jedi is a great movie. Problem is it is not what I wanted to see. It really broke my heart as, my hopes of getting the reunion and continuity with the characters I loved, are now gone.

Disney really don't care about the old fans. They just used our motivation to bring in the new crowd.

The new crowd just needs characters they can relate to. Mixed with Disney's "Everyone can change the world" message, there was no further need for them to "hang on to the past". So lets kill them all off now that they served their purpose.

What I found most annoying was the big buildups they made that ended up being nothing but a wet fart. Snoke, most powerful Sith we have ever seen on screen is so unimportant that he is discarded without any thoughts. Rey, who is she, a Kenodi, a Skywalker, Ben Solo's sister? What a big buildup to revel she is nobody.

They wanted to surprise people so much they made the equivalent of :"thank goodness it was only a dream" plot twist. Yeah sure, I was surprised... but at what cost?

All fans wanted to see was simple, predictable and a good overall story. Snoke is Darth Plagueis, Rey is a Kenobi, Luke trains a new force user and finds the most powerful balance in the force. (A balance between light and darkness) Big show down with the baddy. Convert Ben Solo back to the grey side. And restore peace to the galaxy. Heck, why not bring back Han Solo since people have survived being cut in half by a light saber before...

But I guess that story was too predictable to produce although it would have provided proper closure to the old fans.

Instead, Han is dead, Luke is dead (from an aneurysm or something), Carry Fisher has passed away so safe to say Lea is dead. There is basically nothing left for me to hang on to.

I will likely watch the next movies but my emotional attachment is gone. I don't really care what comes next or when.

They should have just called it a Star Wars Story and reserve the main cast for another movie instead of calling it Star Wars 7-8-9. Fans would have reacted a lot better.

Right, old fans aside, if you didn't have any emotional ties to the old characters, the movie was great. My wife, who was introduced to SW 2 years ago, loved it. She was on the edge of her seat the hole time.

P.S. This is what everyone gets for taking a huge dump on Lucas. He would have done a better job for the old fans because he cared about the characters he created.

Pushing aside the Jar-Jar Binks and poor love scenes, I enjoyed the first trilogy as it was still in the spirit of what I had grown to love. (By the way, C3PO was also annoying in second trilogy only we were kids back then so it didn't affect us.)

title: The Fall and Decline of Star Wars
review:
To quote George Lucas, "there is no Episode VII." And by the transitive property there is no Episode VII. This is not Star Wars. This is an expensive fan fiction film.

I truly don't know where to begin with this train wreck of a movie. Let's get one thing out of the way. This film allegedly takes place about a day after the prior film. In case you don't recall, Starkiller Base was destroyed and the First Order was on the ropes. However the film's opening crawl claims "THE FIRST ORDER REIGNS." How did they gain such an advantage in the course of 24 hours? Is the struggle between the "Resistance" and First Order like a basketball game. Where the advantage keeps going back and forth between the two? In ESB we're given some exposition that the Empire has been chasing the Rebels and has driven them to Hoth. The film opens with a fleet of Star Destroyers chasing the Resistance fleet and never lets up. This film is one big chase scene filled with forgettable dialogue, dull characters, and zero tension.

Rey's training goes very well with Luke. She faces little to no adversity while learning the ways of the force. Aside from Luke's reluctance to train her. Unlike Yoda's playful banter in testing Luke, he comes off as mean spirited and like an old man who's pissed she's on his lawn. There are no moments of self doubt, like Luke had. He had to confront his own fear and failure while becoming a Jedi. Luke's confrontation with the apparition of Vader gave Luke a glimpse into what he could become. And Rey gets a hall of mirrors style carnival trick which made little to no sense. Oh, and Rey's parents are space hobos or drunks or something like that. They're nobodies, after an entire movie's worth of mystery and her desperate wait for her parents, we find out they're just space trash.

And Luke's character is betrayed by the lazy writing. In ROTJ he felt the conflict in Vader and wanted to turn him to the light side and redeem him. And after an emotional battle with Vader where he reveals that Leia is his twin sister, he is forced into a rage and nearly kills his father while Palpatine goads him on. Only when he realizes that he is giving into the dark side he throws his weapon aside and refuses to kill his father. That's when Luke knew he did everything within his own power to redeem his father. In TLJ he mentions trying to kill Kylo Ren in his sleep because he had a thought that he might be evil. Give me a break! The Luke from the previous films would have realized he could still save his nephew and try to turn him to the light side without resorting to murder.

And speaking of Kylo Ren, he's as whiny and conflicted as ever. He killed his father in cold blood. He couldn't do the same with Leia. He had the chance but didn't pull the trigger, literally. There is no great loss that he experienced like Anakin, losing his mother, being denied love with Padme, and initially being turned down by the Jedi council. There is no conflict that would force him to turn to the dark side. And his relationship with Snoke is pretty pathetic. Snoke is just a throwaway villain, like Phasma, looks interesting but there is not substance to them.

As I said earlier the movie is one chase scene. And Finn & Rose's subplot to the casino planet is just that. Tasked to enlist an expert code breaker, who is a high roller, to stop the First Order from tracking them, they arrive on the planet and get busted for parking on the beach. Seriously, they parked in a red zone. Although it might be cliched and overly done a high stakes card against the code breaker could have been a decent distraction from the constant chases. Rose could have used her pendant as collateral to buy into the game. Like it was said on the Simpsons, "it may not bring in much cash. But the sentimental value is through the roof." A family heirloom vs the fate of the galaxy could have brought some tension to the film. Instead we got a lecture on the evil one percent of the galaxy, another on animal rights, a done to hell jail break, all wedged between two Looney Tunes style chase scenes. And I didn't see any Hutts in the casino. Aren't they supposed to be gangsters and obsessed with gambling. That might have made up for some of this useless plot line.

And since this movie is completely out to ruin Star Wars with its Social Justice Agenda and identity politics, I'd like to point out that I could care less about a character's gender identity, sexual orientation, race, ethnicity or whatever as long as there is good story to be told. This film introduces us to Vice Admiral Holdo, after Leia is rendered unconscious and somehow Mary Poppins her way through the cold vacuum of space back to safety. A little character development can go a long way. We're supposed to trust her to save the Resistance and act as a foil to Poe Dameron's maverick pilot. If she were introduced earlier commanding a ship and taking out enemy forces she would be a more believable character. If we saw her in action and turning the tide for the Resistance it could have helped the film move forward. Much like Phasma is a female villain just to be a female villain, Holdo is a female hero just to be a female hero.

Other thoughts are as follows. General Hux is a JROTC cadet who has been given command of an aircraft carrier. He's only about 35 years old, Iain Glen would have been a better choice he's a year older than the current Chief of Naval Operations, just to give you an idea of how old an Admiral or General should be, and would come off as a much more battle hardened and calculating military officer. Poe Dameron is no Han Solo, no matter how hard they try. Harrison Ford had a natural charisma that breathed life into Solo. He had witty one liners whereas Dameron's humor is forced and lame. Luke Skywalker mentioning Darth Sidious by name was the best part of the movie. I was glad that the prequels were finally sort of mentioned. Rian Johnson was the wrong director for this film. Ang Lee would have been a better choice. He's won two best director's Oscars, Brokeback Mountain and The Life of Pi. The latter of which featured massive special effects. He could have brought some much needed prestige to the film.

In conclusion, please avoid!

title: A movie that is about balance. For both film and fans.
review:
"Star Wars: The Last Jedi" is the eight episode and the ninth film in the "Star Wars" saga. It is written and directed by Rian Johnson and stars Mark Hamill returning as Luke Skywalker, Carrie Fisher returns as Leia and is her last role, Daisy Ridley as Rey, John Boyega as Finn, Oscar Issac as Poe Damoren, and Adam Driver as Kylo Ren. The film also stars Keli Marie Tran, Laura Dern, Benicio Del Toro, Domhnall Gleeson, Andy Serkis and many more actors returning their roles.

As the Resistance try to escape from the clutches of the First Order, Rey has found Luke Skywalker and pleaded with him for help. Easier said than done when Luke Skywalker, a legend, and master of the Jedi Order is refusing to help with Rey or the Resistance, wanting no part of this war. In the meantime, Kylo Ren has internal conflict and tries to figure where is his place in all this.

Before I start this review, I know I was late to see this movie, and most of you have seen it. But ever since this film was released, the internet has been divisive, and I mean almost to the point of causing a Civil War between the Star Wars fandom. Many people are praising it, and many people are shaming it. I find it ironic that there is some weird balance in this; like the force, one good, one bad. Star Wars in a way is all about the balance of things, be it the force of nature, or a ying and yang.

Here is a film that presented itself with not just callbacks but with new things: ideas, concepts, new planets, modern societies, hell, even the new ways of the force. In itself, without thinking of the controversy of The Force Awakens, this movie is different, original so to speak. The film makes you think of this one way, but it goes to the next.

There is one word to summarize the previous sentences: unpredictable.

The Last Jedi is unpredictable.

And I like it.

The Last Jedi is filled to the brim with great performances, especially from Mark Hamill, great cinematography, exciting action sequences, great score by John Williams, and great twists and turns with the plot.

Please for anyone who saw the film, no spoilers.

I liked Luke Skywalker's story in this. I like that he was a man who was once devoted to a belief in hope, but ultimately realizes that maybe what he learned was a lie. I like that he had personal conflict with himself and tries to hide from his past.

Carrie Fischer gives off her great final role as Leia Organa who kicks ass and takes names. And for those who say about that one particular scene (which I will not mention because of (a) spoilers and (b) will probably cause of flame war in the co I do not think that that was a bad scene; in a way, it almost makes sense.

Rey's story is expanded more in this film as she learns more about herself and her past. Along with Kylo Ren who we learn more about his past. The scenes with these two together are great from their dialogue to their interactions. I felt that their story alone together is almost a great theme about balance and how if it works together, it could achieve a greater purpose. I will not say further more with these two, you will have to see it for yourself.

The movie is filled with tension in most scenes. Very thick tension that almost makes your feet go up and down repeatedly.

The film is long though. This would make it the longest Star Wars film to date unless if episode ix tops it. Is the long runtime bad? No I don't think so. But there were two scenes in the film that felt like one of them was the last act and the other was just filler.

Which bring me some of my issues with the movie. I don't necessarily think that these scenes are bad per say; they are enjoyable to look at, and they have their own weight to them, but I think that the scene with Finn and Rose, a new character in the saga, should have been in some small spin off story in a cartoon, because it was really just filler and served no purpose to the story. In the same time, I don't think the filler scenes were bad itself. I think they were good scenes because in someway they expand the Star Wars universe a bit further and not with your typical Star Wars fashion but more of something that was more grounded and relatable with our own real world.

I wish I could say more, but I really enjoyed The Last Jedi. I do not believe that this movie should have universal hatred just because it was either too different or it wasn't following the expanded universe or it wasn't fitting with their expectations. Star Wars is a film, and a film can be interpreted in many ways. But when it comes to someone who is making a movie that has a massive following and is also a fan himself, only to be shot down because his ideas did not fit their's is a total disrespect for either fandom or filmmaking.

I learned about false expectations the hard way, but I realized that that was my mistake. I didn't like a film because I was expecting something that I was used to seeing, but when I saw the film, it wasn't what I thought I wanted. And in return I disliked it. But then I watched the film again, and again with a different mind set and I realize that the source material is not mine to control, because I didn't create it. My expectations were selfish and personal, but in some way those expectations could be bad ideas that could hurt a film.

The point is this: don't watch a movie, expecting your speculations and believing that those speculations might come out as true. You would be in for either something good or something disappointing.

The Last Jedi is not disappointing. It was fantastic and I applaud it for its unpredictability and new ideas.

"Star Wars: The Last Jedi" gets an 8.5 out of 10.

title: Thank you for motivating me to become a better storyteller
review:
I'll keep this short and hopefully sweet - if you've read other Last Jedi reviews from fans that were disappointed, you've seen the same themes pop up A) Stupid twists and gotcha moments all over the place that don't advance the story but rather, make it feel like a waste of time to be watching it B) Not playing off of or respecting what came before it, which serves the dual role of i. diminishing those films if we are to accept this film and any others after it and ii. makes this film either seem like it's the ending of a trilogy, or the beginning of a new one, when newsflash, it's the MIDDLE CONNECTING PIECE C) Stupid humor and jokes - this film comes off as a poor man's Guardians of the Galaxy without the excitement, characterization or good storytelling.

Above all else, Disney screwed themselves for episode 9 - characters are the biggest 'assets' you have when it comes to storytelling. For 2 movies (or 4.5 hours of screen time) the new Star Wars trilogy has had to balance introducing new characters while simultaneously including old ones. Because this new trilogy is disconnected and it couldn't make up it's mind, here's what we have to show for it A) New characters are underdeveloped, have virtually no character development or 'hero's journey', and B) Gutting the original characters or using them poorly. Now going into episode 9, we have basically no old characters left in the mix and all the new ones are either uninteresting, underdeveloped, and they have NOTHING LEFT TO RESOLVE. Rey is the least interesting protagonist in a long time because the audience doesn't go through a classic hero's journey with them... no struggles on learning how to pilot a ship, on learning warfare strategy, on learning how to use the force, on learning how to use a light saber and best a sith lord, etc. No pain... no gain. Our protagonist comes to us fresh out of the box ready to go. There's also no larger internal or emotional story or wound that needs to be healed because of how they botched her family in writing this story - what's left to resolve???? What is that big bad thing being held over Rey that she will be incomplete until she resolves it? With Luke, after learning who his father was, it was DESTINY to confront his father come hell or high water to see if he could turn him back to the light in the face of insurmountable odds. What is there for Rey?

Anyways, this was a painful film watching experience because of the missed opportunities. So many wonderful, amazing moments that Rian Johnson could have capitalized on - but didn't. The iron was hot and it was all over the place - he's drawing from one of the most densely populated creative realms (Star Wars) and he botched virtually every moment he had to deliver.

My message to Rian Johnson - we get it, you are a special unique artistic filmmaker 'genius' snowflake who is probably rationalizing the fan reception as "We are morons", "We don't get it", "We are fanboys", etc. What I want to say to that is STAR WARS does not belong to you. Star Wars is NOT about you. It's bigger than you. It's bigger than all of us. When you get pegged to deliver a Star Wars film, you are like the curator of a museum. You are the tour guide - deliver and showcase the goods and step the hell out of the way. Rian Johnson fundamentally didn't understand the place that this franchise has with it's millions of fans. He thought it was about him. It's not. It's not Rian, and as a result you botched it.

Last note - this film never felt like it 'got off the ground'. In every Star Wars film, there's always that moment when you're like "Alright! Things are about to get real now! Let's go!" When Luke turned to Obi-Wan and Said "I want to learn the ways of the force to become a jedi like my father", it was like "Yeah! Let's go!" In ESB, it was when the Imperial Armada is revealed, they discover Hoth and they're like "That's where them mofos have been hiding! Let's get em!" The original trilogy all had it. This film, doesn't. Everything moves at a slow crawl like it's wading through molasses. The film also fails to deliver any of those moments that when you're walking out of the theater with your buddy, you turn to him and go "...and that part when ______ happened, OMG! I lost my mind! That was awesome!" It's all very meh.

Rian Johnson delivers 2.5 hours of slow plot, bad humor, illogical twists and gotcha moments, underdeveloped characters, and relatively little spectacle. You botched it Rian. You botched it.

title: The quality rises, and the flaws to meet it
review:
Something deep inside us drives us to believe that Disney has delivered on the promise of promises: to make Star Wars great again. Even those who saw through the gloss and deep color-grading of the previous installment, The Force Awakens, to its profound shortcomings, argued that its reliance on detailed plot points from previous chapters was merely a path for winning over fans disenfranchised by the (unfairly-maligned) prequels; soon, we would see the true face of this new generation of Star Wars films.

Now I can finally say that I've seen a "real" Disney Star Wars saga film, and that it's more-or-less what I expected. There were two points I had always maintained - first, that artists who possess true vision don't hide it because they're afraid of what the audience will think. And second, that once you've set your story on target to retell the Original Trilogy, it's difficult to turn the ship around.

To its credit, The Last Jedi has its share of compelling moments, but they're often undermined by mediocre, occasionally even terrible, ones. In this film are ideas of all shades of quality - an intriguing hero and villain friendship, new old plot points, and Yoda setting Jedi texts on fire. Prepare to hear the good, the bad, and the ugly.

The highest praise that can be given to The Last Jedi is that it presents us with something new to experience. In the first act, we find ourselves facing a character setup like none seen in any previous Star Wars installment: a pupil, rejected by her master, finding solace in companionship with the story's main antagonist, also facing rejection from his own master. We watch this relationship as it slowly unfolds, watch Rey's hatred transform to sympathy, watch Kylo flirt with the light. There's a strange chemistry between these two characters, as well as some of the best writing the film has to offer. It seems that it all could be leading up to something new and grand. The problem is that it isn't. About halfway through, we are suddenly watching a sort of mishmash of The Empire Strikes Back and Return of the Jedi. Oh, but it isn't exactly the same: here, Darth Vader, after disposing of the Emperor, walks up to the throne and takes his place. One must ask: what's the point of this story? We've found out nothing we don't already know. Kylo is evil; Rey is good. And nope, she doesn't want to join Kylo as Supreme Leader of the First Order. Is that the pivotal twist it's all been building towards? The main storyline is complemented by less-than-compelling, and in one case, vastly overextended, subplots for Finn and Poe, both of which revolve to some extent around a slow-motion chase through outer space and the attempt to escape undetected to an old Rebel Base using small transports. Considering that the First Order has had the Resistance "tied on the end of a string" all along, the transports come off as totally superfluous. The same plot outcome could've been achieved by having the Resistance flee to the base directly. It would've spared us having to watch Finn and a new character, Rose, run off on a side journey where they get jailed for a parking violation, escape on space llamas, dress up in First Order uniforms and sneak onto a ship, fail their mission, and then miraculously catch back up to everyone.

The result of it all is a relatively inconsequential chapter in the Star Wars saga. One could skip from the end of Episode 7 to the beginning of 9 and find that nothing much has changed. The supposedly pivotal middle chapter of this trilogy is mainly a series of diversions which exist to mask how little of a plan or vision Disney really possesses.

Unlike some viewers, I do see the merit behind Luke's portrayal in this film. In fact, I would argue that some sort of grumpy, disillusioned Luke unwilling to train more Jedi was an ideal concept to employ here. However - and I knew it from the trailers - I don't think the film is able to sufficiently justify his actions.

Director Rian Johnson once said of Luke, "I know he's not hiding on the island. I know he's not a coward. He must be there for a reason that he believes in." Yet this reason continues to proves elusive. Yes, he wants the Jedi to end, and considering what they have produced, there's some sort of sense in this. But it does nothing to explain why he can't leave to help Leia. I think we're meant to believe that he feels he will only make things worse. But his failure (as far as we know, his only one) involves training a Jedi. There are other ways he could help. We know that he's a great pilot, for instance. What is it that allows this character to support such a profound delusion?

Also, Yoda's back. And he's here to burn Jedi texts. While laughing about it. He's doing it to make a point: that Rey possesses all the knowledge and wisdom she'll ever need. (Though apparently the books not being "page-turners" is a factor.) This either means that Rey is now genuinely a "Mary Sue", or that total mastery of the Force comes without study or effort, which essentially removes its grandeur and mystique. If you though midichlorians destroyed the essence of the Force (they didn't; they're just an interface with it), well, think again.

The Last Jedi also has some of the most ill-timed comedy of any Star Wars movie, among which is what is perhaps the worst line in the entire saga: "I know what you're going to say. I changed my hair." It comes during what is thus far one of the most serious and pivotal moments of this trilogy, and manages to completely subvert the intended tone. How are we supposed to take this film seriously when Johnson is intent on "challenging our expectations" by pointlessly breaking our immersion around every turn?

And it's worth noting that every stylistic technique you don't want in a Star Wars movie makes an appearance at least once. You'll see slow motion, flashback, muted audio, and voiceover.

Like last year's Rogue One, The Last Jedi is an experience that leaves you with something worth reflecting on, and yet it isn't meant to be a consistently good and entertaining film as much as a product with enough compelling ideas and moments that people will pay for it. Nonetheless, it's all-too-obvious that this franchise's creator is no longer involved, as these films betray the misunderstandings of characters and tone one might expect in that case. With the Original Trilogy plot points out of the way, and the story more-or-less back to where Return of the Jedi left off, perhaps Disney will take the initiative to create a truly compelling final installment. The world needs another good Star Wars movie. So help us, Disney. You're our only hope.
